items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. Which operation produces the arithmetic mean of four comparable readings?
A. Largest minus smallest
B. Their sum multiplied by four
C. Their sum divided by four
D. The last reading divided by four

2. What does the prefix kilo mean?
A. 1000000
B. 0.001
C. 1000
D. 100

3. Which length is a radius?
A. Centre to circumference
B. Between arbitrary polygon vertices
C. Across a circle through its centre
D. Around the circle

4. Which expression gives triangular area?
A. base × sloping side
B. ½ × base × perpendicular height
C. base × height
D. base + height

5. Which is the SI unit of mass?
A. Pa
B. N
C. W
D. kg

6. Which bearing points east?
A. 270°
B. 180°
C. 000°
D. 090°

7. Which expression is the reciprocal of a nonzero period T?
A. T/2
B. 1/T
C. 2T
D. T²

8. Three repeated times are 9.0 s, 9.2 s and 9.1 s. What is their mean?
A. 3.03 s
B. 9.1 s
C. 27.3 s
D. 0.2 s

9. What is 72 ms in seconds?
A. 0.072 s
B. 72 s
C. 0.72 s
D. 72000 s

10. A square has side 0.50 m. What is its area?
A. 2.0 m²
B. 0.50 m²
C. 1.0 m²
D. 0.25 m²

11. What percentage is 9 J out of 30 J?
A. 30%
B. 300%
C. 3.33%
D. 0.30%

12. What is 6.284 rounded to three significant figures?
A. 6.3
B. 6.284
C. 6.28
D. 6.29
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key C. A: This gives the range. B: This scales the total instead of averaging it. C: The total is shared across the number of readings. D: This discards the other readings.

2. Key C. A: This is the mega factor. B: This is the milli factor. C: Kilo multiplies the unit by 10³. D: This is not the kilo factor.

3. Key A. A: A radius starts at the centre. B: That describes neither a circle radius nor its fixed endpoints. C: That is a diameter. D: That is circumference length.

4. Key B. A: The height must be perpendicular and a half is needed. B: The triangular region is half the matching parallelogram. C: This misses the factor one half. D: Adding lengths does not give area.

5. Key D. A: A pascal measures pressure. B: A newton measures force. C: A watt measures power. D: The kilogram measures mass.

6. Key D. A: This points west. B: This points south. C: This points north. D: Bearings are clockwise from north.

7. Key B. A: Halving is not taking a reciprocal. B: The reciprocal reverses the ratio. C: Doubling is not taking a reciprocal. D: Squaring is not taking a reciprocal.

8. Key B. A: This divides a single representative reading by three. B: The sum 27.3 s divided by three is 9.1 s. C: This is the sum, before division. D: This is the range.

9. Key A. A: Milliseconds are divided by 1000. B: The prefix has been ignored. C: This uses the wrong factor. D: This changes in the wrong direction.

10. Key D. A: This is numerically the perimeter, with the wrong unit. B: This leaves the side value unchanged. C: This adds two sides instead of multiplying. D: The product is 0.50 × 0.50.

11. Key A. A: The ratio is 0.30, or thirty per hundred. B: This introduces an extra factor of ten. C: This reverses the ratio and misuses percent. D: This omits multiplication by 100.

12. Key C. A: This gives two significant figures. B: This keeps four significant figures. C: The next digit is 4, so the retained hundredths digit stays unchanged. D: This rounds upward despite the next digit being less than five.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark for the correct option in each question, for 12 marks total.
Distractor feedback: the canonical answer explains the quantity, mechanism or calculation error behind every wrong option.

items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Elapsed time / s is vertical and Oscillation count horizontal. Use the six readings, draw a separate best-fit line and show a wide gradient triangle; do not join scattered readings in a zigzag.

Gradient construction: choose the separated fitted-line points (5, 8) and (30, 48). Gradient = (48 − 8) / (30 − 5) = 1.6 s per oscillation. The slope is the period: elapsed time divided by number of full oscillations, 1.6 s.

Arrangement: A small-angle pendulum on a secured clamp stand, a stopwatch and a fixed fiducial mark

Plan: 1. Measure pendulum length from pivot to bob centre and secure the stand. 2. Displace by a small angle and release without a push. 3. Start the stopwatch as the bob passes the reference mark in a chosen direction. 4. Count 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30 full returns in that same direction and record elapsed times. 5. Repeat each timing at least three times and record every raw reading before finding a mean.
Control and accuracy: Keep string length and release angle fixed. Count consistently at the same reference; keep the swinging bob clear of people.
Table: Oscillation count; Elapsed time / s; repeat readings in separate columns. 
Graph and conclusion: The slope is the period: elapsed time divided by number of full oscillations, 1.6 s. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

![Original fitted practice graph](assets/practical-6118-1.png)
marking_guidance: (a) Correct quantities and units on both axes (1); regular usable scales (1); points within half a small square, all six (2) or four/five (1); a separate suitable fitted line (1).

(b) A visible wide triangle or two stated separated line coordinates (1); difference in vertical coordinates divided by difference in horizontal coordinates, with correct sign and result (1); unit s per oscillation or a stated equivalent derived from vertical unit / horizontal unit (1).
(c) Equipment/arrangement (1): A small-angle pendulum on a secured clamp stand, a stopwatch and a fixed fiducial mark

(c) Measurements (3): One mark each for: Displace by a small angle and release without a push.; Count 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30 full returns in that same direction and record elapsed times.; Repeat each timing at least three times and record every raw reading before finding a mean.

(c) Controls/precaution (2): one mark for a named variable AND how it is kept fixed; one for another specific control or a relevant precaution with its action. Keep string length and release angle fixed. Count consistently at the same reference; keep the swinging bob clear of people.
(c) Table (1): Oscillation count; Elapsed time / s; repeat readings in separate columns.

(c) Analysis/conclusion (1): The slope is the period: elapsed time divided by number of full oscillations, 1.6 s. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

Accept a physically equivalent operational method using suitable named equipment. Do not award a second graph-construction mark in (c). For later calculations, allow error carried forward from a plausible measured gradient when the subsequent relation is correct; do not reward a reversed axis interpretation. Proposed teaching rubric, not a reconstructed official mark scheme.

items.prompt: Explain the link between choosing a suitable instrument and obtaining a useful experimental reading.
items.canonical_answer: Its range and scale must suit the expected quantity. Correct arrangement and reading then allow the intended value, rather than an accidental artefact, to be measured.
marking_guidance: Credit 1 (1): Instrument range/resolution suited to quantity.
Credit 2 (1): Correct setup/reading makes the result represent that quantity; require the link, not just two instrument names.

Maximum 2 marks. Accept equivalent scientifically correct wording or a labelled representation of the same points. Count each distinct idea once; an unsupported keyword alone is not a causal explanation.
The link must include a reason or result connecting the stated ideas; unrelated facts do not earn explanation credit.

items.prompt:
Investigation aim: test water temperature as heating time increases at a fixed heater setting. These are invented, idealised practice readings; real readings have scatter.

| Heating time / s | Temperature / °C |
|---:|---:|
| 0 | 22 |
| 30 | 24.4 |
| 60 | 26.8 |
| 90 | 29.2 |
| 120 | 31.6 |
| 150 | 34 |

(a) Draw Temperature / °C vertically against Heating time / s horizontally. Plot the supplied readings and add a separate fitted line. [5]
(b) Show two widely separated points on your fitted line and calculate its gradient. State the gradient unit. [3]
(c) Plan how to test water temperature as heating time increases at a fixed heater setting. Name the equipment and arrangement, describe the measurements and repeats, state controls and a relevant precaution, design the results table and explain how the results answer the aim. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Temperature / °C is vertical and Heating time / s horizontal. Use the six readings, draw a separate best-fit line and show a wide gradient triangle; do not join scattered readings in a zigzag.

Gradient construction: choose the separated fitted-line points (0, 22) and (150, 34). Gradient = (34 − 22) / (150 − 0) = 0.08 °C/s. The slope is temperature rise per second, 0.08 °C/s, not electrical power.

Arrangement: A 6 V immersion heater in a measured water mass, insulated beaker, thermometer, stirrer and stopwatch

Plan: 1. Measure 100 g of water into the insulated beaker and immerse the rated 6 V heater before switching it on. 2. Place the thermometer in the water away from the heater and beaker wall and record initial temperature. 3. Start the stopwatch with heating and maintain the same supply voltage and heater setting. 4. Stir gently and record temperature every 30 s for 150 s without removing the thermometer. 5. Repeat with fresh water at the same starting temperature and record all repeats.
Control and accuracy: Keep heater power and water mass fixed; stir gently for a representative water temperature and handle hot apparatus safely.
Table: Heating time / s; Temperature / °C; repeat readings in separate columns. 
Graph and conclusion: The slope is temperature rise per second, 0.08 °C/s, not electrical power. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

![Original fitted practice graph](assets/practical-6118-2.png)
marking_guidance: (a) Correct quantities and units on both axes (1); regular usable scales (1); points within half a small square, all six (2) or four/five (1); a separate suitable fitted line (1).

(b) A visible wide triangle or two stated separated line coordinates (1); difference in vertical coordinates divided by difference in horizontal coordinates, with correct sign and result (1); unit °C/s or a stated equivalent derived from vertical unit / horizontal unit (1).
(c) Equipment/arrangement (1): A 6 V immersion heater in a measured water mass, insulated beaker, thermometer, stirrer and stopwatch

(c) Measurements (3): One mark each for: Place the thermometer in the water away from the heater and beaker wall and record initial temperature.; Stir gently and record temperature every 30 s for 150 s without removing the thermometer.; Repeat with fresh water at the same starting temperature and record all repeats.

(c) Controls/precaution (2): one mark for a named variable AND how it is kept fixed; one for another specific control or a relevant precaution with its action. Keep heater power and water mass fixed; stir gently for a representative water temperature and handle hot apparatus safely.
(c) Table (1): Heating time / s; Temperature / °C; repeat readings in separate columns.

(c) Analysis/conclusion (1): The slope is temperature rise per second, 0.08 °C/s, not electrical power. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

Accept a physically equivalent operational method using suitable named equipment. Do not award a second graph-construction mark in (c). For later calculations, allow error carried forward from a plausible measured gradient when the subsequent relation is correct; do not reward a reversed axis interpretation. items.prompt:
Investigation aim: measure a model vehicle’s speed from position and time. These are invented, idealised practice readings; real readings have scatter.

| Time / s | Position / cm |
|---:|---:|
| 0 | 5 |
| 2 | 11 |
| 4 | 17 |
| 6 | 23 |
| 8 | 29 |
| 10 | 35 |

(a) Draw Position / cm vertically against Time / s horizontally. Plot the supplied readings and add a separate fitted line. [5]
(b) Show two widely separated points on your fitted line and calculate its gradient. State the gradient unit. [3]
(c) Plan how to measure a model vehicle’s speed from position and time. Name the equipment and arrangement, describe the measurements and repeats, state controls and a relevant precaution, design the results table and explain how the results answer the aim. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Position / cm is vertical and Time / s horizontal. Use the six readings, draw a separate best-fit line and show a wide gradient triangle; do not join scattered readings in a zigzag.

Gradient construction: choose the separated fitted-line points (0, 5) and (10, 35). Gradient = (35 − 5) / (10 − 0) = 3 cm/s. The slope is speed, 3 cm/s. The 5 cm position intercept does not change speed.

Arrangement: A low-speed trolley on a level track with a metre rule and a phone or camera recording the scale and a visible timer

Plan: 1. Set the camera square to a visible centimetre scale along the level track. 2. Record the trolley moving at a fixed low drive setting with the timer or frame rate known. 3. Choose a starting frame as t = 0 and record the trolley reference point position. 4. Read positions at 2 s intervals from the recording using the same reference point. 5. Repeat the run at the same setting and record the corresponding positions in repeat columns.
Control and accuracy: Keep the track arrangement, drive setting and starting position matched; reduce parallax by reading the scale consistently.
Table: Time / s; Position / cm; repeat readings in separate columns. 
Graph and conclusion: The slope is speed, 3 cm/s. The 5 cm position intercept does not change speed. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

![Original fitted practice graph](assets/practical-6118-3.png)
marking_guidance: (a) Correct quantities and units on both axes (1); regular usable scales (1); points within half a small square, all six (2) or four/five (1); a separate suitable fitted line (1).

(b) A visible wide triangle or two stated separated line coordinates (1); difference in vertical coordinates divided by difference in horizontal coordinates, with correct sign and result (1); unit cm/s or a stated equivalent derived from vertical unit / horizontal unit (1).
(c) Equipment/arrangement (1): A low-speed trolley on a level track with a metre rule and a phone or camera recording the scale and a visible timer

(c) Measurements (3): One mark each for: Record the trolley moving at a fixed low drive setting with the timer or frame rate known.; Read positions at 2 s intervals from the recording using the same reference point.; Repeat the run at the same setting and record the corresponding positions in repeat columns.

(c) Controls/precaution (2): one mark for a named variable AND how it is kept fixed; one for another specific control or a relevant precaution with its action. Keep the track arrangement, drive setting and starting position matched; reduce parallax by reading the scale consistently.
(c) Table (1): Time / s; Position / cm; repeat readings in separate columns.

(c) Analysis/conclusion (1): The slope is speed, 3 cm/s. The 5 cm position intercept does not change speed. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

Accept a physically equivalent operational method using suitable named equipment. Do not award a second graph-construction mark in (c). For later calculations, allow error carried forward from a plausible measured gradient when the subsequent relation is correct; do not reward a reversed axis interpretation. Proposed teaching rubric, not a reconstructed official mark scheme.

items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. Which vessel gives a range of contained liquid-volume readings from graduations along its cylindrical open body?
A. Burette
B. Volumetric flask
C. Pipette
D. Measuring cylinder

2. Which caliper feature measures the inside width of an opening?
A. External jaws
B. Depth rod
C. Internal jaws
D. Main scale alone

3. Why is a micrometer ratchet useful?
A. It helps limit measuring force
B. It prevents all thermal expansion
C. It increases scale resolution
D. It corrects zero error

4. What counts as one full pendulum oscillation?
A. Return to the same position and direction
B. Travel from one extreme to the other
C. Any crossing of the centre
D. Any visible movement

5. Which quantity is scalar?
A. Force
B. Velocity
C. Displacement
D. Energy

6. What additional information distinguishes a vector from a scalar magnitude?
A. Whether it is measured experimentally
B. Whether it changes
C. Direction
D. Whether a unit exists

7. In a tip-to-tail construction, where does the resultant begin?
A. At the first tip along the second vector
B. At the first vector’s original tail
C. From first tail to second tail
D. At the final tip toward the first tail

8. A rod extends from 2.0 cm to 10.7 cm on a ruler. What is its length?
A. 12.7 cm
B. 5.35 cm
C. 10.7 cm
D. 8.7 cm

9. A 0.1 mm vernier gives 12 mm on the main scale and alignment at division 4. With no zero error, what is the reading?
A. 12.4 mm
B. 11.6 mm
C. 16 mm
D. 12.04 mm

10. A micrometer sleeve shows 4.5 mm and the thimble adds 0.18 mm. With no zero error, what is the result?
A. 18.45 mm
B. 4.18 mm
C. 4.68 mm
D. 4.32 mm

11. Twenty complete cycles take 32.0 s. What is the period?
A. 0.625 s
B. 1.60 s
C. 640 s
D. 32.0 s

12. Two perpendicular forces have magnitudes 5 N and 12 N. What is the resultant magnitude?
A. 17 N
B. 13 N
C. 7 N
D. 169 N
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key D. A: Measures delivered rather than contained volume, and the stem specifies a volume contained in an open graduated vessel. B: Calibrated for a single mark rather than a range of readings. C: Delivers one set volume rather than the stated graduated-vessel reading. D: Its graduations report volume.

2. Key C. A: Touch outside surfaces. B: Measures depth rather than internal width. C: They contact the inner surfaces. D: Displays a reading but does not contact the inside faces.

3. Key A. A: This reduces excessive squeezing of the sample. B: Temperature still affects dimensions. C: Resolution comes from screw pitch and scale. D: Zero correction needs a separate zero check.

4. Key A. A: Both position and direction identify a completed cycle. B: This is half a cycle. C: The opposite-direction crossing occurs after half a cycle. D: The interval must be defined.

5. Key D. A: Force is a vector. B: Velocity includes direction. C: Displacement includes direction. D: It has magnitude without a direction.

6. Key C. A: Both kinds can be measured. B: Either kind can change. C: Direction is part of the vector specification. D: Scalars can have units too.

7. Key B. A: This is the second component rather than the resultant. B: It connects the overall start to the final tip. C: This omits the second vector's displacement. D: This reverses the resultant.

8. Key D. A: This adds the endpoint positions. B: Halving one endpoint has no measurement basis. C: This assumes a zero start. D: Subtract the starting position.

9. Key A. A: Add four times 0.1 mm to 12 mm. B: There is no stated correction requiring subtraction. C: This treats divisions as millimetres. D: This assumes a 0.01 mm resolution.

10. Key C. A: This misreads the scales as decimal strings. B: This misses the half-millimetre sleeve value. C: Add the two scale contributions. D: This subtracts instead of adding.

11. Key B. A: This reverses the quotient. B: Divide the elapsed time by twenty. C: This multiplies instead of dividing. D: This is the time of the whole sequence.

12. Key B. A: This would add collinear same-direction magnitudes. B: Pythagoras gives the right-triangle resultant. C: This subtracts magnitudes without the stated directions. D: This omits the square root and has the wrong dimensional interpretation.

(a) Mass is a scalar.

(b) A return to the same position and direction in the repeated motion.

(c) Starting and stopping delays contribute a smaller fraction of the longer timed interval; dividing by 25 estimates one period.

(d) The period is 37.5/25 = 1.50 s.

(e) The magnitude is √(9² + 12²) = 15 m.

(b) One mark for a complete cycle rather than a half-cycle.
(c) One mark for the longer interval reducing relative reaction-time influence; one for division by the correct cycle count.
(d) One mark for dividing by 25; one for 1.50 s.
(e) One mark for the squared-component relation; one for 15 m.

items.prompt:
Investigation aim: measure pendulum period and compare it at different string lengths. These are invented, idealised practice readings; real readings have scatter.

| Oscillation count | Elapsed time / s |
|---:|---:|
| 5 | 7 |
| 10 | 14 |
| 15 | 21 |
| 20 | 28 |
| 25 | 35 |
| 30 | 42 |

(a) Draw Elapsed time / s vertically against Oscillation count horizontally. Plot the supplied readings and add a separate fitted line. [5]
(b) Show two widely separated points on your fitted line and calculate its gradient. State the gradient unit. [3]
(c) Plan how to measure pendulum period and compare it at different string lengths. Name the equipment and arrangement, describe the measurements and repeats, state controls and a relevant precaution, design the results table and explain how the results answer the aim. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Elapsed time / s is vertical and Oscillation count horizontal. Use the six readings, draw a separate best-fit line and show a wide gradient triangle; do not join scattered readings in a zigzag.

Gradient construction: choose the separated fitted-line points (5, 7) and (30, 42). Gradient = (42 − 7) / (30 − 5) = 1.4 s per oscillation. The slope is period, 1.4 s; use the same timing procedure at other lengths to test length dependence.

Arrangement: A clamp stand, thread, bob, metre rule, stopwatch and a fixed reference mark

Plan: 1. Measure length from pivot to bob centre and record it. 2. Release the bob from a small measured angle without pushing. 3. Start and stop the stopwatch at the same mark and direction after a counted set of full oscillations. 4. Repeat for several counts to obtain the elapsed-time versus count line. 5. Repeat the period measurement at new recorded lengths, keeping bob and release angle fixed.
Control and accuracy: Keep pivot-to-centre length and small release angle fixed; avoid pushing the bob and keep its swing clear of people.
Table: Oscillation count; Elapsed time / s; repeat readings in separate columns. 
Graph and conclusion: The slope is period, 1.4 s; use the same timing procedure at other lengths to test length dependence. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

![Original fitted practice graph](assets/practical-6118-4.png)
marking_guidance: (a) Correct quantities and units on both axes (1); regular usable scales (1); points within half a small square, all six (2) or four/five (1); a separate suitable fitted line (1).

(b) A visible wide triangle or two stated separated line coordinates (1); difference in vertical coordinates divided by difference in horizontal coordinates, with correct sign and result (1); unit s per oscillation or a stated equivalent derived from vertical unit / horizontal unit (1).
(c) Equipment/arrangement (1): A clamp stand, thread, bob, metre rule, stopwatch and a fixed reference mark

(c) Measurements (3): One mark each for: Release the bob from a small measured angle without pushing.; Repeat for several counts to obtain the elapsed-time versus count line.; Repeat the period measurement at new recorded lengths, keeping bob and release angle fixed.

(c) Controls/precaution (2): one mark for a named variable AND how it is kept fixed; one for another specific control or a relevant precaution with its action. Keep pivot-to-centre length and small release angle fixed; avoid pushing the bob and keep its swing clear of people.
(c) Table (1): Oscillation count; Elapsed time / s; repeat readings in separate columns.

(c) Analysis/conclusion (1): The slope is period, 1.4 s; use the same timing procedure at other lengths to test length dependence. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

Accept a physically equivalent operational method using suitable named equipment. Do not award a second graph-construction mark in (c). For later calculations, allow error carried forward from a plausible measured gradient when the subsequent relation is correct; do not reward a reversed axis interpretation. items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. Which quantity is the full length of a travelled path?
A. Displacement
B. Distance
C. Velocity
D. Acceleration

2. With east positive, what does position −6 m indicate?
A. Six metres west of the origin
B. That the object is slowing
C. A speed of 6 m/s west
D. A negative path distance

3. Which expression gives average velocity?
A. Time / displacement
B. Velocity change / time
C. Total distance / total time
D. Net displacement / total time

4. What does a horizontal speed-time line above zero show?
A. Rest
B. Steady nonzero speed
C. Uniform deceleration
D. Uniform positive acceleration

5. Which unit measures acceleration?
A. m/s²
B. N
C. m/s³
D. m/s

6. What does negative acceleration alone identify?
A. Speed must rise
B. Its direction under the chosen sign convention
C. Motion must be westward
D. Speed must fall

7. When can v = u + at and s = ut + ½at² describe a straight-line journey?
A. For any varying acceleration without modification
B. Only when the object starts from rest
C. Only when all signs are positive
D. When acceleration is constant

8. A learner walks 10 m east then 4 m west. What is the net displacement?
A. 14 m east
B. 0 m
C. 6 m east
D. 6 m west

9. An object travels 36 m in 6 s then 12 m in 6 s. What is its average speed?
A. 6 m/s
B. 2 m/s
C. 8 m/s
D. 4 m/s

10. Velocity changes from 4 m/s to 10 m/s in 3 s. What is the average acceleration?
A. 2 m/s²
B. 14 m/s²
C. 3.33 m/s²
D. 18 m/s²

11. Speed is 5 m/s for 4 s. What distance is represented by that speed-time rectangle?
A. 1.25 m
B. 10 m
C. 20 m
D. 9 m

12. From rest, an object has constant acceleration 1.5 m/s² for 4 s. What is its displacement?
A. 24 m
B. 3 m
C. 12 m
D. 6 m
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key B. A: This measures the directed start-to-finish change. B: Distance adds the path lengths. C: This is a rate, not a path length. D: This describes velocity change per time.

2. Key A. A: The negative coordinate locates the position west of the reference. B: A position coordinate does not determine acceleration. C: Position is not a velocity. D: Path length is a different quantity.

3. Key D. A: This reverses the physical ratio. B: This is average acceleration. C: This is average speed. D: Both direction and the complete interval matter.

4. Key B. A: Rest has zero speed. B: The vertical value is a speed that is not changing. C: This gives a falling speed-time line. D: This gives a rising speed-time line.

5. Key A. A: Velocity changes by metres per second during each second. B: This is force. C: This is rate of acceleration change, not acceleration. D: This is velocity.

6. Key B. A: Acceleration can instead oppose velocity. B: The effect on speed also depends on velocity direction. C: Acceleration sign does not determine current velocity. D: Speed falls only when acceleration opposes velocity.

7. Key D. A: That violates their condition. B: They allow a nonzero u. C: Consistent signed components are permitted. D: Both equations assume acceleration remains unchanged during the interval.

8. Key C. A: This is the total path length with a direction incorrectly attached. B: The learner has not returned to the starting point. C: Subtract the opposing displacement components. D: This reverses the net direction.

9. Key D. A: This uses the first stage alone. B: This uses the second stage alone. C: This adds stage speeds instead of averaging the full journey. D: The total is 48 m in 12 s.

10. Key A. A: The change is 6 m/s over 3 s. B: This adds the velocities without a time ratio. C: This divides final velocity by time and omits u. D: This multiplies the velocity change by time.

11. Key C. A: This divides speed by time instead of using area. B: This adds an unjustified half factor to a rectangle representing steady speed. C: Speed multiplied by duration gives the rectangular area. D: This adds unlike quantities.

12. Key C. A: This omits the factor one half. B: This does not account for the time-squared factor. C: Use one half times acceleration times time squared. D: This is the final speed value with the wrong dimension.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark for the correct option in each question, for 12 marks total.
Distractor feedback: the canonical answer explains the quantity, mechanism or calculation error behind every wrong option.

items.prompt:
Original structured practice. Answer the parts with working and units where needed.

(a) State whether displacement is scalar or vector. [1]

(b) State the SI unit of acceleration. [1]

(c) Explain why a horizontal distance-time line indicates rest whereas a horizontal speed-time line at 2 m/s does not. [2]

(d) Calculate the constant acceleration for a speed increase from 1 to 7 m/s in 3 s without changing direction. [2]

(e) Calculate the travelled distance for that uniform speed increase from 1 to 7 m/s during 3 s. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Displacement is a vector.

(b) m/s²

(c) The distance-time line has zero gradient and hence zero speed. A horizontal nonzero speed-time line directly states steady motion.

(d) The acceleration is (7 − 1)/3 = 2 m/s² in the direction of motion.

(e) The trapezium area is ½ × (1 + 7) × 3 = 12 m.
marking_guidance: (a) One mark for vector.
(b) One mark for a valid acceleration unit.
(c) One mark for unchanged distance; one for the nonzero speed distinction.
(d) One mark for velocity change divided by time; one for 2 m/s².
(e) One mark for distance = average speed × duration, equivalent constant-acceleration displacement equation, or trapezium area; one for 12 m with unit. Retain method credit after arithmetic error.
Eight marks total; use the definition, reason or working requested by each part.

items.prompt:
Investigation aim: test whether a model trolley has constant acceleration. These are invented, idealised practice readings; real readings have scatter.

| Time / s | Speed / m s⁻¹ |
|---:|---:|
| 0 | 0.1 |
| 1 | 0.3 |
| 2 | 0.5 |
| 3 | 0.7 |
| 4 | 0.9 |
| 5 | 1.1 |

(a) Draw Speed / m s⁻¹ vertically against Time / s horizontally. Plot the supplied readings and add a separate fitted line. [5]
(b) Show two widely separated points on your fitted line and calculate its gradient. State the gradient unit. [3]
(c) Plan how to test whether a model trolley has constant acceleration. Name the equipment and arrangement, describe the measurements and repeats, state controls and a relevant precaution, design the results table and explain how the results answer the aim. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Speed / m s⁻¹ is vertical and Time / s horizontal. Use the six readings, draw a separate best-fit line and show a wide gradient triangle; do not join scattered readings in a zigzag.

Gradient construction: choose the separated fitted-line points (0, 0.1) and (5, 1.1). Gradient = (1.1 − 0.1) / (5 − 0) = 0.2 m/s². The speed-time gradient is acceleration, 0.20 m/s².

Arrangement: A trolley on a fixed shallow ramp, metre scale and fixed camera with a known frame rate

Plan: 1. Fix a metre scale beside the ramp and a camera square to the trolley path. 2. Record a trolley run with the frame rate known and identify a reproducible starting frame. 3. Read trolley positions at equal frame intervals and record both positions and times. 4. Calculate each interval speed as distance change divided by interval time and assign it to the interval midpoint. 5. Repeat the release and readings with the same ramp slope and trolley.
Control and accuracy: Keep the track slope and drive setting matched between repeats; secure the track and keep the run clear.
Table: Time / s; Speed / m s⁻¹; repeat readings in separate columns. 
Graph and conclusion: The speed-time gradient is acceleration, 0.20 m/s². Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

![Original fitted practice graph](assets/practical-6118-5.png)
marking_guidance: (a) Correct quantities and units on both axes (1); regular usable scales (1); points within half a small square, all six (2) or four/five (1); a separate suitable fitted line (1).

(b) A visible wide triangle or two stated separated line coordinates (1); difference in vertical coordinates divided by difference in horizontal coordinates, with correct sign and result (1); unit m/s² or a stated equivalent derived from vertical unit / horizontal unit (1).
(c) Equipment/arrangement (1): A trolley on a fixed shallow ramp, metre scale and fixed camera with a known frame rate

(c) Measurements (3): One mark each for: Record a trolley run with the frame rate known and identify a reproducible starting frame.; Calculate each interval speed as distance change divided by interval time and assign it to the interval midpoint.; Repeat the release and readings with the same ramp slope and trolley.

(c) Controls/precaution (2): one mark for a named variable AND how it is kept fixed; one for another specific control or a relevant precaution with its action. Keep the track slope and drive setting matched between repeats; secure the track and keep the run clear.
(c) Table (1): Time / s; Speed / m s⁻¹; repeat readings in separate columns.
(c) Analysis/conclusion (1): The speed-time gradient is acceleration, 0.20 m/s². Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

Accept a physically equivalent operational method using suitable named equipment. Do not award a second graph-construction mark in (c). For later calculations, allow error carried forward from a plausible measured gradient when the subsequent relation is correct; do not reward a reversed axis interpretation. Proposed teaching rubric, not a reconstructed official mark scheme.

items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. What is the direction of a normal contact force?
A. Parallel to surface
B. Perpendicular to the contact surface
C. Opposite weight for that interaction
D. Along resultant force

2. Which interaction is tension?
A. A taut string pulling a load
B. Earth attracting a stone
C. A table pressing perpendicular to a book
D. Air slowing a falling object

3. A cart moves with constant velocity. What is its resultant force in a constant-mass model?
A. Downward weight
B. Sum of force magnitudes
C. Forward driving force
D. Zero

4. What is spring extension?
A. Loaded length
B. Loaded plus unloaded length
C. Unloaded minus loaded length
D. Loaded length minus unloaded length

5. Where does the limit of proportionality occur?
A. Where elastic return first becomes imperfect
B. At the largest measured force regardless of shape
C. Where the initial proportional graph trend ends
D. Where spring finally breaks

6. What condition permits a system’s total momentum to be conserved?
A. No external resultant force
B. Equal masses of colliding bodies
C. No kinetic energy loss
D. Zero total momentum initially

7. Which unit represents momentum?
A. kg m/s²
B. J/s
C. kg m/s
D. N/m

8. Forces of 17 N east and 5 N west act on one body. What is their resultant?
A. 22 N east
B. 12 N east
C. 0 N
D. 12 N west

9. A spring within its proportional range has k = 80 N/m and extension 0.025 m. What is the force?
A. 2.0 N
B. 0.0003125 N
C. 80.025 N
D. 3200 N

10. A 4 kg object has a 10 N resultant force. What is its acceleration?
A. 0.4 m/s²
B. 2.5 m/s²
C. 40 m/s²
D. 10 m/s²

11. A 0.30 kg trolley moves at 4 m/s east. What is its momentum?
A. 1.2 kg m/s west
B. 0.075 kg m/s east
C. 1.2 kg m/s east
D. 13.3 kg m/s east

12. An average resultant of 8 N acts east for 0.25 s. What momentum change does it cause?
A. 8.25 N s east
B. 0 N s
C. 32 N s east
D. 2 N s east
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key B. A: That is a tangential force. B: The normal direction is defined by the surface. C: Normal follows surface geometry, not always vertical. D: The resultant may combine several directions.

2. Key A. A: The string transmits a pull along itself. B: That is gravitational force. C: That is normal contact. D: That is drag.

3. Key D. A: Support balances weight. B: Resultant is a signed/vector sum. C: Resistive forces balance it. D: Zero acceleration implies zero resultant.

4. Key D. A: Unloaded length must be subtracted. B: Sum includes the original length twice. C: This gives the wrong sign for extension. D: It is the increase in length.

5. Key C. A: Elastic limit and proportional limit are distinct. B: Departure from straight proportional trend is the criterion. C: The force/extension ratio ceases to be constant. D: Breakage is a later condition.

6. Key A. A: This excludes a net external momentum transfer. B: Unequal masses can also conserve momentum. C: Momentum can be conserved in an inelastic collision. D: A system may conserve nonzero momentum.

7. Key C. A: This is a force unit. B: This is power. C: Momentum is mass times velocity. D: This can represent spring stiffness.

8. Key B. A: This adds opposing magnitudes. B: The opposing components subtract. C: The forces are unequal. D: This reverses the stronger direction.

9. Key A. A: Use F = kx. B: This reverses the ratio. C: This adds quantities with different units. D: This divides instead of multiplying.

10. Key B. A: This reverses the quotient. B: Divide resultant force by mass. C: This multiplies force and mass. D: This ignores the stated mass.

11. Key C. A: This reverses the momentum direction. B: This divides mass by velocity. C: Multiply mass by velocity and retain direction. D: This divides velocity by mass.

12. Key D. A: This adds incompatible quantities. B: A nonzero external resultant over time changes momentum. C: This divides by time. D: Multiply force by its duration.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark for the correct option in each question, for 12 marks total.
Distractor feedback: the canonical answer explains the quantity, mechanism or calculation error behind every wrong option.

items.prompt:
Investigation aim: test spring extension as applied force increases within its elastic range. These are invented, idealised practice readings; real readings have scatter.

| Force / N | Extension / mm |
|---:|---:|
| 0 | 0 |
| 0.2 | 2.4 |
| 0.4 | 4.8 |
| 0.6 | 7.2 |
| 0.8 | 9.6 |
| 1 | 12 |

(a) Draw Extension / mm vertically against Force / N horizontally. Plot the supplied readings and add a separate fitted line. [5]
(b) Show two widely separated points on your fitted line and calculate its gradient. State the gradient unit. [3]
(c) Plan how to test spring extension as applied force increases within its elastic range. Name the equipment and arrangement, describe the measurements and repeats, state controls and a relevant precaution, design the results table and explain how the results answer the aim. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Extension / mm is vertical and Force / N horizontal. Use the six readings, draw a separate best-fit line and show a wide gradient triangle; do not join scattered readings in a zigzag.

Gradient construction: choose the separated fitted-line points (0, 0) and (1, 12). Gradient = (12 − 0) / (1 − 0) = 12 mm/N. The slope is extension per force, 12 mm/N. Stiffness is its reciprocal: 1/0.012 = about 83 N/m.

Arrangement: A clamped spring, pointer, millimetre ruler, mass hanger and slotted masses with a stated g

Plan: 1. Clamp the spring securely and align a millimetre ruler with its pointer. 2. Record unloaded pointer length. 3. Add 20 g masses in steps up to 100 g including the hanger as appropriate, using the stated g = 10 N/kg to calculate force. 4. Wait for oscillations to settle at each force, read pointer length squarely and subtract unloaded length. 5. Unload in the same steps and record repeat lengths to check return to the original position.
Control and accuracy: Use the same spring and reference point, read the scale perpendicularly and protect against falling loads or overload.
Table: Force / N; Extension / mm; repeat readings in separate columns. 
Graph and conclusion: The slope is extension per force, 12 mm/N. Stiffness is its reciprocal: 1/0.012 = about 83 N/m. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

![Original fitted practice graph](assets/practical-6118-6.png)
marking_guidance: (a) Correct quantities and units on both axes (1); regular usable scales (1); points within half a small square, all six (2) or four/five (1); a separate suitable fitted line (1).

(b) A visible wide triangle or two stated separated line coordinates (1); difference in vertical coordinates divided by difference in horizontal coordinates, with correct sign and result (1); unit mm/N or a stated equivalent derived from vertical unit / horizontal unit (1).
(c) Equipment/arrangement (1): A clamped spring, pointer, millimetre ruler, mass hanger and slotted masses with a stated g

(c) Measurements (3): One mark each for: Record unloaded pointer length.; Wait for oscillations to settle at each force, read pointer length squarely and subtract unloaded length.; Unload in the same steps and record repeat lengths to check return to the original position.

(c) Controls/precaution (2): one mark for a named variable AND how it is kept fixed; one for another specific control or a relevant precaution with its action. Use the same spring and reference point, read the scale perpendicularly and protect against falling loads or overload.
(c) Table (1): Force / N; Extension / mm; repeat readings in separate columns.

(c) Analysis/conclusion (1): The slope is extension per force, 12 mm/N. Stiffness is its reciprocal: 1/0.012 = about 83 N/m. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

Accept a physically equivalent operational method using suitable named equipment. Do not award a second graph-construction mark in (c). For later calculations, allow error carried forward from a plausible measured gradient when the subsequent relation is correct; do not reward a reversed axis interpretation. items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. Which unit represents mass?
A. N
B. Pa
C. kg
D. N/kg

2. Which property is associated with resistance to a change of motion?
A. Density
B. Momentum
C. Weight
D. Inertia

3. What is gravitational field strength?
A. Weight per mass
B. Weight per volume
C. Mass divided by weight
D. Weight times mass

4. At downward terminal velocity, what is the resultant on the falling body?
A. Weight downward
B. Zero
C. Weight plus drag magnitudes
D. Drag upward

5. Which expression gives density?
A. Mass times volume
B. Weight divided by volume
C. Volume divided by mass
D. Mass / volume

6. Which defect makes the displacement volume of a fully submerged solid too large?
A. Reading initial level too high
B. Losing liquid while lowering the object
C. Failing to immerse the object fully
D. Trapped bubbles on the submerged object

7. At approximately what temperature is liquid water densest?
A. 10 °C
B. 20 °C
C. 4 °C
D. 0 °C

8. What is the weight of a 0.60 kg sample where g = 10 N/kg?
A. 6.0 N
B. 6.0 kg
C. 0.060 N
D. 600 N

9. A sample weighs 4.5 N in a 10 N/kg field. What is its mass?
A. 4.5 kg
B. 45 kg
C. 0.45 kg
D. 0.45 N

10. A mass of 36 g occupies 12 cm³. What is its density?
A. 0.333 cm³/g
B. 3 g/cm³
C. 24 g/cm³
D. 432 g/cm³

11. A vessel is 22 g empty and 70 g with liquid. What is the liquid mass?
A. 70 g
B. 48 g
C. 22 g
D. 92 g

12. An immersed solid raises water from 28 to 37 cm³. What is its volume?
A. 9 cm³
B. 65 cm³
C. 28 cm³
D. 37 cm³
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key C. A: Newtons measure force. B: This measures pressure. C: Mass is measured in kilograms. D: This is gravitational field strength.

2. Key D. A: This is mass per volume. B: This depends on velocity as well as mass. C: This is gravitational force. D: Mass is associated with inertia.

3. Key A. A: This gives g = W/m. B: That is not force per mass. C: This is reciprocal field strength. D: The correct ratio is W/m.

4. Key B. A: Drag balances it at terminal speed. B: Drag and weight balance. C: Opposite forces must be subtracted. D: Weight balances this force.

5. Key D. A: Density is a ratio. B: Weight is not mass. C: This is reciprocal density. D: It compares the mass with occupied volume.

6. Key D. A: This subtracts too much and underestimates the displacement. B: This reduces the final level, underestimating displacement. C: This displaces too little liquid. D: They can increase the apparent displaced volume.

7. Key C. A: Warming above 4 °C lowers its density. B: This is not the density maximum. C: This is the maximum-density region. D: Water's liquid density maximum is near 4 °C.

8. Key A. A: Multiply mass by field strength. B: This reports force as a mass. C: This divides by g. D: This mishandles the mass scale.

9. Key C. A: This equates the numerical force and mass. B: This multiplies instead of dividing. C: Divide weight by g. D: This retains a force unit for a mass result.

10. Key B. A: This is reciprocal density. B: Divide 36 by 12. C: This subtracts unlike quantities. D: This multiplies mass and volume.

11. Key B. A: This includes the vessel. B: Subtract the empty-vessel mass. C: This is the empty-vessel mass alone. D: This adds the two measured masses.

12. Key A. A: Use the volume increase. B: This adds the levels. C: This is the starting water volume. D: This includes the original water.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark for the correct option in each question, for 12 marks total.
Distractor feedback: the canonical answer explains the quantity, mechanism or calculation error behind every wrong option.

items.prompt:
Original structured practice. Answer the parts with working and units where needed.

(a) State the SI unit of mass. [1]

(b) State a suitable unit for density when mass is in grams and volume in cubic centimetres. [1]

(c) Explain why the mass of an empty vessel must be subtracted when finding liquid density. [2]

(d) Calculate the density of 28 g of liquid occupying 35 cm³. [2]

(e) Calculate the weight of a 1.8 kg sample where g = 10 N/kg. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) kg

(b) g/cm³

(c) The combined mass includes material that is not part of the liquid volume. Subtraction isolates the mass of the sample whose volume is measured.

(d) The density is 28/35 = 0.80 g/cm³.

(e) W = mg = 18 N.
marking_guidance: (a) One mark for kilogram or kg.
(b) One mark for grams per cubic centimetre.
(c) One mark for recognising the unwanted vessel mass; one for isolating the matched liquid mass.
(d) One mark for mass divided by volume; one for 0.80 g/cm³.
(e) One mark for multiplying by g; one for 18 N.
Eight marks total; use the definition, reason or working requested by each part.

items.prompt:
Investigation aim: measure the density of a light mineral-oil sample. These are invented, idealised practice readings; real readings have scatter.

| Volume / cm³ | Mass / g |
|---:|---:|
| 5 | 4 |
| 10 | 8 |
| 15 | 12 |
| 20 | 16 |
| 25 | 20 |
| 30 | 24 |

(a) Draw Mass / g vertically against Volume / cm³ horizontally. Plot the supplied readings and add a separate fitted line. [5]
(b) Show two widely separated points on your fitted line and calculate its gradient. State the gradient unit. [3]
(c) Plan how to measure the density of a light mineral-oil sample. Name the equipment and arrangement, describe the measurements and repeats, state controls and a relevant precaution, design the results table and explain how the results answer the aim. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Mass / g is vertical and Volume / cm³ horizontal. Use the six readings, draw a separate best-fit line and show a wide gradient triangle; do not join scattered readings in a zigzag.

Gradient construction: choose the separated fitted-line points (5, 4) and (30, 24). Gradient = (24 − 4) / (30 − 5) = 0.8 g/cm³. The mass-versus-volume gradient is density, 0.80 g/cm³ = 800 kg/m³. Total container-plus-liquid mass would instead have a container-mass intercept.

Arrangement: A balance, dry beaker, measuring cylinder and a room-temperature light mineral-oil sample; keep away from ignition sources

Plan: 1. Check the balance zero and weigh the dry empty beaker. 2. Measure 5 cm³ of the mineral oil in the cylinder, reading its meniscus squarely. 3. Transfer to the beaker, weigh beaker plus oil and subtract empty-beaker mass. 4. Repeat for 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30 cm³ total volumes, recording the oil mass for each. 5. Repeat volume and mass measurements with a dry container and record the repeated results.
Control and accuracy: Use the same liquid at a similar temperature and the same dry container; correct tare and avoid bubbles or spills.
Table: Volume / cm³; Mass / g; repeat readings in separate columns. 
Graph and conclusion: The mass-versus-volume gradient is density, 0.80 g/cm³ = 800 kg/m³. Total container-plus-liquid mass would instead have a container-mass intercept. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

![Original fitted practice graph](assets/practical-6118-7.png)
marking_guidance: (a) Correct quantities and units on both axes (1); regular usable scales (1); points within half a small square, all six (2) or four/five (1); a separate suitable fitted line (1).

(b) A visible wide triangle or two stated separated line coordinates (1); difference in vertical coordinates divided by difference in horizontal coordinates, with correct sign and result (1); unit g/cm³ or a stated equivalent derived from vertical unit / horizontal unit (1).
(c) Equipment/arrangement (1): A balance, dry beaker, measuring cylinder and a room-temperature light mineral-oil sample; keep away from ignition sources

(c) Measurements (3): One mark each for: Measure 5 cm³ of the mineral oil in the cylinder, reading its meniscus squarely.; Repeat for 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30 cm³ total volumes, recording the oil mass for each.; Repeat volume and mass measurements with a dry container and record the repeated results.

(c) Controls/precaution (2): one mark for a named variable AND how it is kept fixed; one for another specific control or a relevant precaution with its action. Use the same liquid at a similar temperature and the same dry container; correct tare and avoid bubbles or spills.
(c) Table (1): Volume / cm³; Mass / g; repeat readings in separate columns.

(c) Analysis/conclusion (1): The mass-versus-volume gradient is density, 0.80 g/cm³ = 800 kg/m³. Total container-plus-liquid mass would instead have a container-mass intercept. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

Accept a physically equivalent operational method using suitable named equipment. Do not award a second graph-construction mark in (c). For later calculations, allow error carried forward from a plausible measured gradient when the subsequent relation is correct; do not reward a reversed axis interpretation. Proposed teaching rubric, not a reconstructed official mark scheme.

items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. Which change increases the moment for the same perpendicular force?
A. Smaller perpendicular arm
B. A larger pivot-to-force-line distance
C. Same arm and reversed force
D. Same arm with a different force direction closer to the arm

2. Which quantity has magnitude but no direction?
A. Momentum
B. Force
C. Velocity
D. Work

3. In scissors, which part serves as fulcrum?
A. The joint
B. The material
C. The fingers
D. The blade tip

4. Which pair of conditions establishes equilibrium?
A. Zero force alone
B. Zero resultant force and moment
C. Zero moment alone
D. A large support force alone

5. Where is the centre of mass of a freely suspended stationary lamina?
A. On the vertical below the suspension point
B. At the lowest corner
C. At the suspension hole
D. At the largest visible edge

6. Which change usually improves resistance to toppling?
A. Moving load toward edge
B. Widening the support base
C. Raising centre of mass
D. Narrowing base

7. Which use needs substantial friction?
A. Reducing heating in a lubricated bearing
B. Letting a machine slide with less heating
C. Reducing wheel-bearing wear
D. A brake pad stopping a wheel

8. What moment does 8 N produce with a 0.15 m perpendicular arm?
A. 120 N m
B. 53.3 N m
C. 1.2 N m
D. 0.01875 N m

9. A 4 N load has a 0.30 m arm. What load balances it on a 0.20 m opposing arm?
A. 6 N
B. 2.67 N
C. 12 N
D. 4 N

10. A force line passes through a pivot. What is its moment about that pivot?
A. Equal clockwise and anticlockwise nonzero moments from this one force
B. Force × distance along the beam
C. Force × distance to the nearest end
D. Zero

11. A light beam supports 3 N and 5 N downward and is stationary. What upward support is required?
A. 2 N
B. 10 N
C. 8 N
D. Zero

12. A force holds a stationary lever. What is its work on the lever during the hold?
A. Equal to its moment in joules
B. Force times lever length
C. Zero
D. Its gravitational energy increase
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key B. A: Moment decreases at fixed force. B: Moment equals force times perpendicular arm. C: The moment reverses but its magnitude does not grow. D: The perpendicular component decreases.

2. Key D. A: Momentum includes direction. B: Force includes direction. C: Velocity includes direction. D: It is an energy transfer.

3. Key A. A: The blades rotate about this pivot. B: It supplies the cutting resistance. C: They provide effort. D: It is away from the pivot.

4. Key B. A: A couple can still turn the body. B: Both translation and rotation are balanced. C: Translation can still accelerate. D: Its balance with other forces is unspecified.

5. Key A. A: Its weight line passes through the support. B: The lowest point need not be the centre of mass. C: The body generally hangs below that point. D: Edge length does not locate it.

6. Key B. A: Weight line is closer to the tipping boundary. B: A larger tilt is then needed to move weight beyond it. C: Weight line leaves base after a smaller tilt. D: Support boundary is reached sooner.

7. Key D. A: This calls for reduced friction, unlike braking. B: This calls for less friction. C: This calls for less friction. D: Friction transfers motion energy away.

8. Key C. A: This uses centimetres as metres. B: This divides by distance. C: Multiply 8 by 0.15. D: This reverses the ratio.

9. Key A. A: The required moment is 1.2 N m. B: This reverses the distance ratio. C: This doubles the required balancing force. D: Equal loads need equal arms.

10. Key D. A: The one force has zero moment when its line passes through the pivot. B: Only the perpendicular distance to the force line belongs in a moment. C: The specified pivot, not an arbitrary end, sets the arm. D: The perpendicular arm is zero.

11. Key C. A: The downward loads add rather than subtract. B: This exceeds the 3+5 N downward total and would give an upward resultant. C: Vertical forces balance. D: That would leave a downward resultant.

12. Key C. A: Moment and work are different quantities. B: That length is not a movement. C: The application point has no displacement. D: The stationary lever has no height change during the hold.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark for the correct option in each question, for 12 marks total.
Distractor feedback: the canonical answer explains the quantity, mechanism or calculation error behind every wrong option.

items.prompt:
Investigation aim: test the balance of moments using reciprocal effort against effort arm. These are invented, idealised practice readings; real readings have scatter.

| Effort distance / m | Reciprocal effort / N⁻¹ |
|---:|---:|
| 0.05 | 0.025 |
| 0.1 | 0.05 |
| 0.15 | 0.075 |
| 0.2 | 0.1 |
| 0.25 | 0.125 |
| 0.3 | 0.15 |

(a) Draw Reciprocal effort / N⁻¹ vertically against Effort distance / m horizontally. Plot the supplied readings and add a separate fitted line. [5]
(b) Show two widely separated points on your fitted line and calculate its gradient. State the gradient unit. [3]
(c) Plan how to test the balance of moments using reciprocal effort against effort arm. Name the equipment and arrangement, describe the measurements and repeats, state controls and a relevant precaution, design the results table and explain how the results answer the aim. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Reciprocal effort / N⁻¹ is vertical and Effort distance / m horizontal. Use the six readings, draw a separate best-fit line and show a wide gradient triangle; do not join scattered readings in a zigzag.

Gradient construction: choose the separated fitted-line points (0.05, 0.025) and (0.3, 0.15). Gradient = (0.15 − 0.025) / (0.3 − 0.05) = 0.5 N⁻¹ m⁻¹. The plotted relation is 1/F = d/M. Gradient = 1/M = 0.50 N⁻¹ m⁻¹, so the fixed moment M = 2.0 N m.

Arrangement: A rigid rated beam on a secured pivot, a fixed 10 N load at 0.20 m and a calibrated 0–50 N force gauge; this is not a lightly supported metre rule

Plan: 1. Balance the unloaded rigid beam on its secured pivot and account for its weight. 2. Fix a 10 N load with a 0.20 m perpendicular arm on one side. 3. On the other side attach the 0–50 N force gauge at a measured arm between 0.05 and 0.30 m. 4. Pull vertically and adjust force until the beam is horizontal; record force and arm without hand support elsewhere. 5. Repeat at each arm, recording gauge readings and their reciprocals; restore the same load position each time.
Control and accuracy: Use a beam, support and gauge rated for at least 50 N; secure the fixed load, keep forces vertical and the opposing arm fixed, and keep hands clear of falling loads.
Table: Effort distance / m; Reciprocal effort / N⁻¹; repeat readings in separate columns. Also record raw effort F / N before calculating 1/F / N⁻¹.
Graph and conclusion: The plotted relation is 1/F = d/M. Gradient = 1/M = 0.50 N⁻¹ m⁻¹, so the fixed moment M = 2.0 N m. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

![Original fitted practice graph](assets/practical-6118-8.png)
marking_guidance: (a) Correct quantities and units on both axes (1); regular usable scales (1); points within half a small square, all six (2) or four/five (1); a separate suitable fitted line (1).

(b) A visible wide triangle or two stated separated line coordinates (1); difference in vertical coordinates divided by difference in horizontal coordinates, with correct sign and result (1); unit N⁻¹ m⁻¹ or a stated equivalent derived from vertical unit / horizontal unit (1).
(c) Equipment/arrangement (1): A rigid rated beam on a secured pivot, a fixed 10 N load at 0.20 m and a calibrated 0–50 N force gauge; this is not a lightly supported metre rule

(c) Measurements (3): One mark each for: Fix a 10 N load with a 0.20 m perpendicular arm on one side.; Pull vertically and adjust force until the beam is horizontal; record force and arm without hand support elsewhere.; Repeat at each arm, recording gauge readings and their reciprocals; restore the same load position each time.

(c) Controls/precaution (2): one mark for a named variable AND how it is kept fixed; one for another specific control or a relevant precaution with its action. Use a beam, support and gauge rated for at least 50 N; secure the fixed load, keep forces vertical and the opposing arm fixed, and keep hands clear of falling loads.
(c) Table (1): Effort distance / m; Reciprocal effort / N⁻¹; repeat readings in separate columns. Also record raw effort F / N before calculating 1/F / N⁻¹.

(c) Analysis/conclusion (1): The plotted relation is 1/F = d/M. Gradient = 1/M = 0.50 N⁻¹ m⁻¹, so the fixed moment M = 2.0 N m. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

Accept a physically equivalent operational method using suitable named equipment. Do not award a second graph-construction mark in (c). For later calculations, allow error carried forward from a plausible measured gradient when the subsequent relation is correct; do not reward a reversed axis interpretation. items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. What changes in a chemical fuel reaction?
A. Atomic nuclei change proton numbers
B. Electrons become new nuclei
C. Atoms are rearranged
D. Total mass-energy disappears

2. Which source uses hot rocks beneath Earth’s surface?
A. Tidal
B. Photovoltaic
C. Geothermal
D. Wind

3. Which fuel is finite in the syllabus classification?
A. Nuclear fuel
B. Sunlight
C. Tidal flow
D. Wind

4. Which process supplies the Sun’s energy?
A. Fusion
B. Radioactive decay alone
C. Fission
D. Chemical combustion

5. Which energy change occurs in an illuminated photovoltaic cell?
A. Radiant energy directly to water flow
B. Radiant energy to electrical energy
C. Electrical energy to sunlight
D. Thermal energy to nuclear energy

6. What is the main useful output of a solar water heater?
A. Electrical energy at the collector terminals
B. Chemical energy stored in new fuel
C. Kinetic energy of a rotor
D. Increased water internal energy

7. Which difficulty is particularly associated with fission products?
A. Combustion ash from burning coal
B. Radioactive waste management
C. Wind-turbine blade noise
D. Flooding a reservoir valley

8. A farm needs water after dark. Which arrangement stores daytime solar pumping’s useful result?
A. A raised water tank
B. A smaller unshaded panel without storage
C. Removing the pump
D. A disconnected empty wire

9. A hydroelectric installation keeps the same water fall height and efficiency while water mass flow per second halves. What happens to its output power?
A. It is unchanged
B. It falls to one quarter
C. It doubles
D. It halves

10. A PV refrigerator is operating. Where is energy rejected?
A. Nowhere because cooling destroys energy
B. To the surroundings through the hot side
C. Into a disappearing mass
D. Into the panel as manufactured sunlight

11. A wind project has no fuel combustion during generation. What follows?
A. Its operation never changes habitat
B. Its output stays constant
C. Its operational combustion emissions are avoided
D. Its whole life cycle has no emissions

12. Water rises from 22 to 30 °C in 4 min. What is its average heating rate?
A. 7.5 °C/min
B. 8 °C/min
C. 32 °C/min
D. 2 °C/min
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key C. A: That would be a nuclear change. B: Ordinary chemical reactions rearrange electrons and bonds. C: The chemical products have a different arrangement. D: Products and energy transfers must be included.

2. Key C. A: This uses tidal movement. B: This uses incident radiation. C: It draws on internal thermal energy. D: This uses moving air.

3. Key A. A: Its usable material is a finite resource. B: It is treated as renewable. C: This is renewable on human timescales. D: This is a replenished flow.

4. Key A. A: Light nuclei join in the Sun. B: Fusion supplies the stellar energy in this course. C: Fission splits heavy nuclei, whereas the Sun fuses light nuclei. D: The Sun is not powered by burning chemical fuel.

5. Key B. A: A pump needs an electrical/mechanical pathway. B: The cell converts incident light directly into electrical output. C: This reverses the operating energy pathway. D: A photovoltaic cell does not produce nuclear fuel.

6. Key D. A: A solar thermal collector heats water. B: The stated heater raises water internal energy. C: That is a wind-turbine pathway. D: The intended service is heating.

7. Key B. A: Coal ash is a combustion issue, not the particular fission-product problem. B: Some products need containment over long periods. C: This is a wind-installation issue rather than the named fission-product difficulty. D: Reservoir flooding is associated with hydroelectric construction.

8. Key A. A: The stored water can later flow down. B: It still lacks night illumination. C: This removes the lifting mechanism. D: This stores no useful pumping output.

9. Key D. A: Same energy per kilogram does not mean same energy per second. B: Only one factor has halved, not two. C: Reduced mass flow reduces input energy rate. D: Each kilogram releases the same mgh, but half as many kilograms pass per second.

10. Key B. A: Energy is conserved. B: The removed heat plus input energy must leave. C: The cooling model does not remove material. D: That is not the cooling pathway.

11. Key C. A: Land use, noise and wildlife effects still need consideration. B: Changing wind changes power availability. C: This is the supported claim. D: Construction, transport and maintenance may have emissions.

12. Key D. A: This divides final temperature by time. B: This omits division by the interval. C: This multiplies rise by time. D: The rise is 8 °C over 4 min.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark for the correct option in each question, for 12 marks total.
Distractor feedback: the canonical answer explains the quantity, mechanism or calculation error behind every wrong option.

items.prompt:
Original structured practice. Answer the parts with working and units where needed.

(a) State the energy form carried by wind. [1]

(b) State the useful energy output of a PV panel. [1]

(c) Explain how insulation helps a solar water tank. [2]

(d) Calculate the average heating rate when water warms by 9 °C in 6 min. [2]

(e) Explain why storing water can suit a pump with variable solar output. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Kinetic energy.

(b) Electrical energy.

(c) It reduces energy transfer from hotter water to cooler surroundings, retaining more of the collected energy.

(d) Rate = temperature rise/time = 1.5 °C/min.

(e) Water can be raised while sunlight is available. The tank then supplies water later without the pump operating at that instant.
marking_guidance: (a) One mark for kinetic energy.
(b) One mark for electrical output.
(c) One mark for reduced transfer; one for retaining useful internal energy.
(d) One mark for dividing rise by time; one for 1.5 °C/min.
(e) One mark for collecting the useful result during supply; one for later delivery independent of instantaneous output.
Eight marks total; use the definition, reason or working requested by each part.

items.prompt:
Investigation aim: compare solar-collector water temperature with exposure time. These are invented, idealised practice readings; real readings have scatter.

| Time / min | Water temperature / °C |
|---:|---:|
| 0 | 21 |
| 2 | 22.6 |
| 4 | 24.2 |
| 6 | 25.8 |
| 8 | 27.4 |
| 10 | 29 |

(a) Draw Water temperature / °C vertically against Time / min horizontally. Plot the supplied readings and add a separate fitted line. [5]
(b) Show two widely separated points on your fitted line and calculate its gradient. State the gradient unit. [3]
(c) Plan how to compare solar-collector water temperature with exposure time. Name the equipment and arrangement, describe the measurements and repeats, state controls and a relevant precaution, design the results table and explain how the results answer the aim. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Water temperature / °C is vertical and Time / min horizontal. Use the six readings, draw a separate best-fit line and show a wide gradient triangle; do not join scattered readings in a zigzag.

Gradient construction: choose the separated fitted-line points (0, 21) and (10, 29). Gradient = (29 − 21) / (10 − 0) = 0.8 °C/min. The slope is temperature rise per minute, 0.8 °C/min over this short interval; it is not collector efficiency.

Arrangement: A small solar water collector, measured water mass, thermometer, stirrer and stopwatch under steady illumination

Plan: 1. Measure a fixed water mass into the collector and record its initial temperature. 2. Set the collector at a fixed angle under steady sunlight or a controlled safe lamp. 3. Start a stopwatch when exposure begins. 4. Stir gently before reading temperature every 2 min for 10 min. 5. Repeat with the same water mass and starting temperature under comparable illumination.
Control and accuracy: Hold collector area, angle and water mass fixed; minimise draught changes, avoid looking into intense lamps and handle warm water carefully.
Table: Time / min; Water temperature / °C; repeat readings in separate columns. 
Graph and conclusion: The slope is temperature rise per minute, 0.8 °C/min over this short interval; it is not collector efficiency. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

![Original fitted practice graph](assets/practical-6118-9.png)
marking_guidance: (a) Correct quantities and units on both axes (1); regular usable scales (1); points within half a small square, all six (2) or four/five (1); a separate suitable fitted line (1).

(b) A visible wide triangle or two stated separated line coordinates (1); difference in vertical coordinates divided by difference in horizontal coordinates, with correct sign and result (1); unit °C/min or a stated equivalent derived from vertical unit / horizontal unit (1).
(c) Equipment/arrangement (1): A small solar water collector, measured water mass, thermometer, stirrer and stopwatch under steady illumination

(c) Measurements (3): One mark each for: Set the collector at a fixed angle under steady sunlight or a controlled safe lamp.; Stir gently before reading temperature every 2 min for 10 min.; Repeat with the same water mass and starting temperature under comparable illumination.

(c) Controls/precaution (2): one mark for a named variable AND how it is kept fixed; one for another specific control or a relevant precaution with its action. Hold collector area, angle and water mass fixed; minimise draught changes, avoid looking into intense lamps and handle warm water carefully.
(c) Table (1): Time / min; Water temperature / °C; repeat readings in separate columns.

(c) Analysis/conclusion (1): The slope is temperature rise per minute, 0.8 °C/min over this short interval; it is not collector efficiency. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

Accept a physically equivalent operational method using suitable named equipment. Do not award a second graph-construction mark in (c). For later calculations, allow error carried forward from a plausible measured gradient when the subsequent relation is correct; do not reward a reversed axis interpretation. Proposed teaching rubric, not a reconstructed official mark scheme.

items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. Which store is associated with motion?
A. Kinetic
B. Chemical alone
C. Gravitational alone
D. Strain alone

2. Which distance belongs in W = Fd for a parallel force?
A. Distance to Earth’s centre
B. Width of the object
C. Displacement along the force
D. Perpendicular arm to a pivot

3. What does an efficiency below 100% mean?
A. Some input is not useful output
B. Power must be zero
C. Energy is destroyed
D. Output exceeds input

4. Which unit measures power?
A. kg
B. N
C. W
D. J

5. What is the main ideal effect of a single fixed pulley?
A. Halving effort force
B. Changing effort direction
C. Halving effort distance
D. Doubling output work

6. Why does a real swinging pendulum slow?
A. The period consumes energy by itself
B. Energy transfers to surroundings
C. Mechanical energy is destroyed
D. Gravitational field weakens each swing

7. A small external gear drives a larger one. How does the larger gear turn?
A. Faster in opposite direction
B. Slower in same direction
C. Faster in same direction
D. Slower and oppositely

8. What is Ek for 2 kg at 3 m/s?
A. 18 J
B. 3 J
C. 6 J
D. 9 J

9. What energy is gained by 4 kg raised 0.5 m with g = 10 N/kg?
A. 80 J
B. 20 J
C. 200 J
D. 2 J

10. A 5 N force acts along 4 m. What work does it do?
A. 9 J
B. 0.8 J
C. 20 J
D. 1.25 J

11. Useful output is 90 J from 150 J input. What is efficiency?
A. 167%
B. 90%
C. 40%
D. 60%

12. What average power transfers 240 J in 8 s?
A. 30 W
B. 0.033 W
C. 240 W
D. 1920 W
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key A. A: It depends on mass and speed. B: This concerns material configuration. C: This depends on height. D: This depends on deformation.

2. Key C. A: That is not the work distance here. B: It need not be a displacement. C: This is the work distance. D: This belongs to moment.

3. Key A. A: Other stores or surroundings receive it. B: Useful transfer may still occur. C: Total energy is conserved. D: That reverses the comparison.

4. Key C. A: This measures mass. B: This measures force. C: One watt is one joule per second. D: This measures energy.

5. Key B. A: Single fixed pulley changes direction, not ideal force. B: It does not reduce force in the simple model. C: Effort distance equals load rise in this arrangement. D: An ideal pulley conserves work.

6. Key B. A: Dissipative interactions cause the loss. B: Drag and friction reduce mechanical energy. C: Energy transfers to surroundings instead. D: Friction and drag explain the damping.

7. Key D. A: Larger driven gear rotates slower. B: External meshed gears turn oppositely. C: Both speed and direction changes are wrong. D: Its larger circumference requires more tooth movement per turn.

8. Key D. A: This omits the half. B: This fails to square speed. C: This uses mv rather than energy. D: Half times 2 times 3 squared is 9.

9. Key B. A: This divides by height. B: Use mgh. C: This misplaces a factor of ten. D: This omits g.

10. Key C. A: Adding unlike quantities does not give work. B: This reverses that ratio. C: Multiply force by displacement. D: This divides force by distance.

11. Key D. A: This reverses the ratio. B: This ignores total input. C: This is the non-useful fraction. D: The useful fraction is 0.6.

12. Key A. A: Divide energy by time. B: This uses time per energy. C: This ignores duration. D: This multiplies by time.

items.prompt:
Investigation aim: measure useful power during a steady vertical lift. These are invented, idealised practice readings; real readings have scatter.

| Time / s | Gravitational energy gained / J |
|---:|---:|
| 0 | 0 |
| 2 | 6 |
| 4 | 12 |
| 6 | 18 |
| 8 | 24 |
| 10 | 30 |

(a) Draw Gravitational energy gained / J vertically against Time / s horizontally. Plot the supplied readings and add a separate fitted line. [5]
(b) Show two widely separated points on your fitted line and calculate its gradient. State the gradient unit. [3]
(c) Plan how to measure useful power during a steady vertical lift. Name the equipment and arrangement, describe the measurements and repeats, state controls and a relevant precaution, design the results table and explain how the results answer the aim. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Gravitational energy gained / J is vertical and Time / s horizontal. Use the six readings, draw a separate best-fit line and show a wide gradient triangle; do not join scattered readings in a zigzag.

Gradient construction: choose the separated fitted-line points (0, 0) and (10, 30). Gradient = (30 − 0) / (10 − 0) = 3 J/s or W. The energy-time gradient is useful lifting power, 3 W; the electrical or human input power can be greater.

Arrangement: A guarded hand-operated lifting mechanism, a 3.0 kg secured load, metre rule and stopwatch; at g = 10 N/kg a 1.0 m rise gains 30 J

Plan: 1. Secure the 3.0 kg load in a rated guarded manual hoist and set a vertical metre rule beside it. 2. Record starting height and the stated g = 10 N/kg. 3. Raise the load steadily through up to 1.0 m while a second observer times the lift. 4. Record height gained at 2 s intervals and calculate mgh at each time. 5. Lower safely and repeat the run with the same mass and lifting rate.
Control and accuracy: Keep mass and lifting arrangement fixed; avoid acceleration intervals and secure the load against falling.
Table: Time / s; Gravitational energy gained / J; repeat readings in separate columns. 
Graph and conclusion: The energy-time gradient is useful lifting power, 3 W; the electrical or human input power can be greater. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

![Original fitted practice graph](assets/practical-6118-10.png)
marking_guidance: (a) Correct quantities and units on both axes (1); regular usable scales (1); points within half a small square, all six (2) or four/five (1); a separate suitable fitted line (1).

(b) A visible wide triangle or two stated separated line coordinates (1); difference in vertical coordinates divided by difference in horizontal coordinates, with correct sign and result (1); unit J/s or W or a stated equivalent derived from vertical unit / horizontal unit (1).
(c) Equipment/arrangement (1): A guarded hand-operated lifting mechanism, a 3.0 kg secured load, metre rule and stopwatch; at g = 10 N/kg a 1.0 m rise gains 30 J

(c) Measurements (3): One mark each for: Record starting height and the stated g = 10 N/kg.; Record height gained at 2 s intervals and calculate mgh at each time.; Lower safely and repeat the run with the same mass and lifting rate.

(c) Controls/precaution (2): one mark for a named variable AND how it is kept fixed; one for another specific control or a relevant precaution with its action. Keep mass and lifting arrangement fixed; avoid acceleration intervals and secure the load against falling.
(c) Table (1): Time / s; Gravitational energy gained / J; repeat readings in separate columns.

(c) Analysis/conclusion (1): The energy-time gradient is useful lifting power, 3 W; the electrical or human input power can be greater. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

Accept a physically equivalent operational method using suitable named equipment. Do not award a second graph-construction mark in (c). For later calculations, allow error carried forward from a plausible measured gradient when the subsequent relation is correct; do not reward a reversed axis interpretation.
