items.prompt:
Investigation aim: determine sound speed from wall-echo timing. These are invented, idealised practice readings; real readings have scatter.

| Round-trip time / s | Reflector distance / m |
|---:|---:|
| 0.1 | 17 |
| 0.2 | 34 |
| 0.3 | 51 |
| 0.4 | 68 |
| 0.5 | 85 |
| 0.6 | 102 |

(a) Draw Reflector distance / m vertically against Round-trip time / s horizontally. Plot the supplied readings and add a separate fitted line. [5]
(b) Show two widely separated points on your fitted line and calculate its gradient. State the gradient unit. [3]
(c) Plan how to determine sound speed from wall-echo timing. Name the equipment and arrangement, describe the measurements and repeats, state controls and a relevant precaution, design the results table and explain how the results answer the aim. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Reflector distance / m is vertical and Round-trip time / s horizontal. Use the six readings, draw a separate best-fit line and show a wide gradient triangle; do not join scattered readings in a zigzag.

Gradient construction: choose the separated fitted-line points (0.1, 17) and (0.6, 102). Gradient = (102 − 17) / (0.6 − 0.1) = 170 m/s. The one-way reflector distance versus round-trip time slope is c/2 = 170 m/s. Therefore sound speed c = 340 m/s.

Arrangement: A large flat wall, measuring tape and a microphone with audio recorder or timing display; a long-distance repeated-clap stopwatch method is an alternative

Plan: 1. Measure the perpendicular source-to-wall distance with a tape and place the microphone beside the source. 2. Make a short moderate click and record direct and echo pulses on the audio timing display. 3. Read the time separation of the pulse peaks, not the total recording length. 4. Repeat several times at the same distance and record the delays. 5. Repeat at several distances; alternatively time many clap–echo cycles with a stopwatch at a large known distance and divide by the cycle count.
Control and accuracy: Keep air conditions similar, avoid competing reflectors, do not use harmful sound levels and account for electronic timing offsets.
Table: Round-trip time / s; Reflector distance / m; repeat readings in separate columns. 
Graph and conclusion: The one-way reflector distance versus round-trip time slope is c/2 = 170 m/s. Therefore sound speed c = 340 m/s. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

![Original fitted practice graph](assets/practical-6118-20.png)
marking_guidance: (a) Correct quantities and units on both axes (1); regular usable scales (1); points within half a small square, all six (2) or four/five (1); a separate suitable fitted line (1).

(b) A visible wide triangle or two stated separated line coordinates (1); difference in vertical coordinates divided by difference in horizontal coordinates, with correct sign and result (1); unit m/s or a stated equivalent derived from vertical unit / horizontal unit (1).
(c) Equipment/arrangement (1): A large flat wall, measuring tape and a microphone with audio recorder or timing display; a long-distance repeated-clap stopwatch method is an alternative

(c) Measurements (3): One mark each for: Make a short moderate click and record direct and echo pulses on the audio timing display.; Repeat several times at the same distance and record the delays.; Repeat at several distances; alternatively time many clap–echo cycles with a stopwatch at a large known distance and divide by the cycle count.

(c) Controls/precaution (2): one mark for a named variable AND how it is kept fixed; one for another specific control or a relevant precaution with its action. Keep air conditions similar, avoid competing reflectors, do not use harmful sound levels and account for electronic timing offsets.
(c) Table (1): Round-trip time / s; Reflector distance / m; repeat readings in separate columns.

(c) Analysis/conclusion (1): The one-way reflector distance versus round-trip time slope is c/2 = 170 m/s. Therefore sound speed c = 340 m/s. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

Accept a physically equivalent operational method using suitable named equipment. Do not award a second graph-construction mark in (c). For later calculations, allow error carried forward from a plausible measured gradient when the subsequent relation is correct; do not reward a reversed axis interpretation. items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. A rod loses electrons while rubbed with a cloth. Which pair describes their net charges?
A. Rod positive, cloth negative
B. Both neutral
C. Rod negative, cloth positive
D. Both positive

2. What unit measures charge?
A. V
B. C
C. A
D. W

3. What do two negative charges do?
A. Exert no force without contact
B. Attract because signs match
C. Lose their charge automatically
D. Repel

4. Which is a typical conductor?
A. Copper
B. Dry wood
C. Dry glass
D. Dry rubber

5. What does a precipitator collect?
A. Charged particles from a gas
B. Uncharged dust without first charging it
C. Neutral pollutant gas by simple mechanical sieving
D. Water vapour by cooling alone

6. Field direction is defined using which test charge?
A. No specified sign
B. Positive
C. Negative
D. Neutral only

7. Can a neutral electroscope deflect when a charged rod approaches without contact?
A. Yes, because electrons are created at the leaf
B. Yes, by redistribution
C. Yes, because the rod must touch it
D. No, a neutral conductor cannot separate charge internally

8. A material gains electrons. What net charge can result?
A. It depends only on the rod mass
B. Positive
C. Negative
D. Neutral regardless of the gain

9. A charged rod attracts neutral paper. What is supported?
A. The rod must be neutral
B. The paper must already have opposite net charge
C. Charge has been created without transfer
D. Polarisation can account for attraction

10. A field points right. Which way is electric force on an electron?
A. Upward
B. Right by the positive convention
C. Left
D. Zero due to electron charge

11. During charging by induction with a negative rod kept nearby, which connection is removed first to leave the insulated conductor positive?
A. Disconnect the insulating stand first
B. Remove the rod first
C. Keep Earth connected after removing the rod
D. Earth connection first

12. Where is the simple uniform-plate-field model most appropriate?
A. Next to an isolated point charge
B. At a plate edge
C. Near the central region between broad plates
D. Far outside the plates
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key A. A: Electrons moved from rod to cloth, leaving equal opposite net charges. B: Electron transfer changes the net balance on each object. C: This reverses the stated electron-transfer direction. D: Transfer leaves one electron deficit and one excess.

2. Key B. A: Volt measures energy per charge. B: Coulomb is the charge unit. C: Ampere measures current. D: Watt measures power.

3. Key D. A: Electrostatic force acts at a distance. B: Like signs repel. C: Approach alone does not neutralise equal-sign charges. D: Like signs repel.

4. Key A. A: It has mobile electrons. B: Typically insulating in this comparison. C: Ordinary glass is an insulator. D: Electrons not freely mobile in bulk.

5. Key A. A: An electric force moves them to collectors. B: Charging and electric force are essential stages. C: Electrostatic precipitator targets charged suspended particles. D: That is condensation.

6. Key B. A: A direction convention requires one. B: This is the direction convention. C: Its force is opposite the defined direction. D: It has no simple qE force.

7. Key B. A: Charges move rather than being created. B: Electrons shift so leaf and stem acquire like charge and repel, while total electroscope charge may remain zero. C: Stem explicitly excludes contact. D: Its electrons can redistribute.

8. Key C. A: Charge balance depends on electrons and protons, not mass alone. B: Gaining negative electrons makes net charge more negative. C: Electrons add negative charge. D: A net added electron imbalance changes charge.

9. Key D. A: A charged rod can attract neutral material. B: Attraction alone does not prove that. C: The observation does not require that. D: Opposite nearer induced charge can dominate.

10. Key C. A: Electric force is along or opposite the field, not at right angles to it. B: That convention applies to positive test charge. C: Its charge is negative. D: An electron is charged.

11. Key D. A: The stand is not the charge-flow connection. B: While earth remains, replacement electrons can return. C: This permits neutralisation through Earth. D: Removing earth while the rod remains prevents replacement electrons entering; the rod is removed afterwards.

12. Key C. A: Its field is radial rather than uniform. B: Field lines curve near edges. C: Edge effects are smaller there. D: The simple uniform central pattern is not applicable.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark for the correct option in each question, for 12 marks total.
Distractor feedback: the canonical answer explains the quantity, mechanism or calculation error behind every wrong option.

(b) State the interaction between like charges. [1]

(b) Repulsion.

(e) It traps the intended net charge on the isolated conductor. If the rod is removed first, electrons can return through the earth connection and restore neutrality.

Eight marks total; use the definition, reason or working requested by each part.

B. AC because its size varies
C. AC only during the pulse maximum
D. Neither AC nor DC because it is not constant
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key C. A: Current is rate of flow. B: This is power. C: This gives C/s or A. D: This is voltage.

2. Key D. A: Ammeter must not short a source. B: That parallel meter path can short it. C: This does not measure the specified branch. D: The measured charge flows through it.

3. Key D. A: That would alter the circuit strongly. B: A two-point difference needs both connections. C: It should have high resistance. D: Its terminals compare the resistor’s endpoints.

4. Key B. A: This occurs in metals for AC and DC. B: Alternating current repeatedly reverses direction; variation in magnitude alone is insufficient. C: This is pulsating DC. D: This is DC.

5. Key B. A: Negative sign still applies in steady current. B: Electrons carry negative charge. C: Charge sign reverses direction, not rotates 90°. D: Negative carriers drift opposite convention.

6. Key D. A: Charge per time. B: Energy divided by time, not charge. C: Emf is per unit charge, not total energy. D: It describes the source contribution.

7. Key A. A: Voltage is energy per charge. B: That is 1 A. C: That is 1 W. D: That is 1 Pa.

8. Key C. A: This reverses the ratio. B: This multiplies them. C: Divide charge by time. D: This ignores duration.

9. Key A. A: Use It. B: This divides time by current. C: This ignores duration. D: This divides current by time.

10. Key B. A: This reverses the ratio. B: Divide energy by charge. C: This ignores the amount of charge. D: This multiplies energy and charge.

11. Key C. A: This divides by the number. B: That ignores series addition. C: Their energy-per-charge contributions add. D: They are not opposing one another.

12. Key A. A: One-direction flow is the defining feature. B: AC requires direction reversal. C: Classification follows reversal, not instantaneous size. D: Unidirectional pulsating current is DC.

items.prompt:
Investigation aim: test how voltage depends on the number of identical cells in series. These are invented, idealised practice readings; real readings have scatter.

| Cell count | Potential difference / V |
|---:|---:|
| 1 | 1.45 |
| 2 | 2.9 |
| 3 | 4.35 |
| 4 | 5.8 |
| 5 | 7.25 |
| 6 | 8.7 |

(a) Draw Potential difference / V vertically against Cell count horizontally. Plot the supplied readings and add a separate fitted line. [5]
(b) Show two widely separated points on your fitted line and calculate its gradient. State the gradient unit. [3]
(c) Plan how to test how voltage depends on the number of identical cells in series. Name the equipment and arrangement, describe the measurements and repeats, state controls and a relevant precaution, design the results table and explain how the results answer the aim. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Potential difference / V is vertical and Cell count horizontal. Use the six readings, draw a separate best-fit line and show a wide gradient triangle; do not join scattered readings in a zigzag.

Gradient construction: choose the separated fitted-line points (1, 1.45) and (6, 8.7). Gradient = (8.7 − 1.45) / (6 − 1) = 1.45 V per cell. The slope is open-circuit voltage per series-aiding cell, 1.45 V per cell. Cell count has no physical unit.

Arrangement: Six matched low-voltage cells, holders, connecting leads and a high-resistance DC voltmeter

Plan: 1. Check voltmeter zero and choose a suitable DC range. 2. Put one cell in its holder and connect only the voltmeter across it. 3. Record open-circuit voltage, keeping fingers clear of exposed contacts. 4. Add matched cells series-aiding one at a time up to six and record total voltage at each count. 5. Repeat the count sequence and measure individual cells to check that their voltages are similar.
Control and accuracy: Use similar cells in similar condition, avoid short circuits, keep total voltage within safe classroom limits and do not connect a measuring ammeter across the cells.
Table: Cell count; Potential difference / V; repeat readings in separate columns. 
Graph and conclusion: The slope is open-circuit voltage per series-aiding cell, 1.45 V per cell. Cell count has no physical unit. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

![Original fitted practice graph](assets/practical-6118-22.png)
marking_guidance: (a) Correct quantities and units on both axes (1); regular usable scales (1); points within half a small square, all six (2) or four/five (1); a separate suitable fitted line (1).

(b) A visible wide triangle or two stated separated line coordinates (1); difference in vertical coordinates divided by difference in horizontal coordinates, with correct sign and result (1); unit V per cell or a stated equivalent derived from vertical unit / horizontal unit (1).
(c) Equipment/arrangement (1): Six matched low-voltage cells, holders, connecting leads and a high-resistance DC voltmeter

(c) Measurements (3): One mark each for: Put one cell in its holder and connect only the voltmeter across it.; Add matched cells series-aiding one at a time up to six and record total voltage at each count.; Repeat the count sequence and measure individual cells to check that their voltages are similar.

(c) Controls/precaution (2): one mark for a named variable AND how it is kept fixed; one for another specific control or a relevant precaution with its action. Use similar cells in similar condition, avoid short circuits, keep total voltage within safe classroom limits and do not connect a measuring ammeter across the cells.
(c) Table (1): Cell count; Potential difference / V; repeat readings in separate columns.

(c) Analysis/conclusion (1): The slope is open-circuit voltage per series-aiding cell, 1.45 V per cell. Cell count has no physical unit. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

Accept a physically equivalent operational method using suitable named equipment. Do not award a second graph-construction mark in (c). For later calculations, allow error carried forward from a plausible measured gradient when the subsequent relation is correct; do not reward a reversed axis interpretation. items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. Which unit measures resistance?
A. A
B. V
C. Ω
D. C

2. Under what condition is current proportional to voltage for an ohmic metal conductor?
A. A different material at every reading
B. No current measurement
C. Fixed temperature and physical conditions
D. A steadily heating filament

3. Parallel branches share what?
A. A series-only path
B. Potential difference
C. Equal resistance by definition
D. Equal current regardless of components

4. What does a relay use to operate contacts?
A. A permanent magnet with no current-operated coil
B. A resistor heating contacts to open them
C. A fuse link melting during every operation
D. An electromagnet

5. Why does a filament lamp’s current cease to be proportional to voltage as the voltage is increased?
A. Its temperature and resistance change
B. Its resistance stays fixed while it heats
C. Current uses up charge in the filament
D. The supply voltage must stay zero

6. Which symbol identifies an ammeter?
A. A in a circle
B. A circle with a cross
C. Unequal parallel plates
D. V in a circle

7. What is a diode’s rectifying behaviour?
A. Blocks both directions at all voltages
B. Reverses current periodically by itself
C. Conducts equally in both directions
D. Strongly favours one direction

8. What resistance gives 6 V at 0.5 A?
A. 12 Ω
B. 3 Ω
C. 0.083 Ω
D. 6 Ω

9. What is 5 Ω in series with 8 Ω?
A. 3.08 Ω
B. 13 Ω
C. 40 Ω
D. 3 Ω

10. What is 4 Ω in parallel with 4 Ω?
A. 16 Ω
B. 2 Ω
C. 4 Ω
D. 8 Ω

11. Two branches carry 0.2 A and 0.6 A. What source current feeds them?
A. 0.4 A
B. 0.12 A
C. 0.8 A
D. 3 A

12. A wire’s diameter doubles at unchanged length, material and temperature. What is its resistance factor?
A. One half
B. Four
C. Two
D. One quarter
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key C. A: Ampere is current. B: Volt is potential difference. C: Ohm is V/A. D: Coulomb is charge.

2. Key C. A: That changes the conductor. B: The relation involves current. C: Resistance must remain constant in the comparison. D: Its resistance changes.

3. Key B. A: Parallel creates separate paths. B: They span the same two nodes. C: Components need not match. D: Branch resistances can differ.

4. Key D. A: No switched magnetic actuator for the stated relay. B: Not its electromagnetic control mechanism. C: Relay uses reversible magnetic switching. D: Its coil attracts an armature.

5. Key A. A: Heating changes the current-voltage ratio. B: Temperature changes metal resistance. C: Charge is conserved. D: A lit filament has nonzero voltage.

6. Key A. A: It is the current-measuring instrument. B: That is a lamp. C: That is a cell. D: That is a voltmeter.

7. Key D. A: Forward conduction occurs after knee. B: Rectification follows the applied input, not autonomous generation. C: Ordinary diode characteristic is asymmetric. D: Its characteristic is asymmetric.

8. Key A. A: Use V/I. B: This multiplies V and I. C: This reverses the ratio. D: This ignores current.

9. Key B. A: This is their parallel combination. B: Series resistances add. C: This multiplies without dividing. D: This subtracts.

10. Key B. A: This multiplies branch values. B: Equal parallel branches halve resistance. C: The second path increases ease of current flow. D: That is series addition.

11. Key C. A: This subtracts rather than adds. B: This multiplies currents. C: Branch currents add. D: This divides them.

12. Key D. A: This mistakes diameter for area. B: This reverses the area dependence. C: A thicker wire has lower resistance. D: Area rises by four.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark for the correct option in each question, for 12 marks total.
Distractor feedback: the canonical answer explains the quantity, mechanism or calculation error behind every wrong option.

items.prompt:
Investigation aim: measure a metal resistor’s resistance at approximately fixed temperature. These are invented, idealised practice readings; real readings have scatter.

| Current / A | Potential difference / V |
|---:|---:|
| 0.05 | 0.6 |
| 0.1 | 1.2 |
| 0.15 | 1.8 |
| 0.2 | 2.4 |
| 0.25 | 3 |
| 0.3 | 3.6 |

(a) Draw Potential difference / V vertically against Current / A horizontally. Plot the supplied readings and add a separate fitted line. [5]
(b) Show two widely separated points on your fitted line and calculate its gradient. State the gradient unit. [3]
(c) Plan how to measure a metal resistor’s resistance at approximately fixed temperature. Name the equipment and arrangement, describe the measurements and repeats, state controls and a relevant precaution, design the results table and explain how the results answer the aim. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Potential difference / V is vertical and Current / A horizontal. Use the six readings, draw a separate best-fit line and show a wide gradient triangle; do not join scattered readings in a zigzag.

Gradient construction: choose the separated fitted-line points (0.05, 0.6) and (0.3, 3.6). Gradient = (3.6 − 0.6) / (0.3 − 0.05) = 12 V/A or Ω. With potential difference vertically against current, the slope is resistance, 12 Ω, at approximately fixed temperature.

Arrangement: A 12 Ω resistor rated at least 5 W, current-limited low-voltage DC supply, series ammeter, parallel voltmeter, rheostat and switch

Plan: 1. Connect the 5 W or higher-rated resistor, ammeter, rheostat and switch in series with a low-voltage supply. 2. Connect a high-resistance voltmeter across the test resistor. 3. Set 0.05 A, close the switch briefly and record paired current and voltage. 4. Repeat at 0.10–0.30 A in suitable steps, opening the switch between readings to limit temperature change. 5. Repeat each pair after cooling; use the same resistor and compare V-I slopes.
Control and accuracy: Keep the resistor temperature approximately fixed, use suitable meter ranges and never connect an ammeter directly across the supply.
Table: Current / A; Potential difference / V; repeat readings in separate columns. 
Graph and conclusion: With potential difference vertically against current, the slope is resistance, 12 Ω, at approximately fixed temperature. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

![Original fitted practice graph](assets/practical-6118-23.png)
marking_guidance: (a) Correct quantities and units on both axes (1); regular usable scales (1); points within half a small square, all six (2) or four/five (1); a separate suitable fitted line (1).

(b) A visible wide triangle or two stated separated line coordinates (1); difference in vertical coordinates divided by difference in horizontal coordinates, with correct sign and result (1); unit V/A or Ω or a stated equivalent derived from vertical unit / horizontal unit (1).
(c) Equipment/arrangement (1): A 12 Ω resistor rated at least 5 W, current-limited low-voltage DC supply, series ammeter, parallel voltmeter, rheostat and switch

(c) Measurements (3): One mark each for: Connect a high-resistance voltmeter across the test resistor.; Repeat at 0.10–0.30 A in suitable steps, opening the switch between readings to limit temperature change.; Repeat each pair after cooling; use the same resistor and compare V-I slopes.

(c) Controls/precaution (2): one mark for a named variable AND how it is kept fixed; one for another specific control or a relevant precaution with its action. Keep the resistor temperature approximately fixed, use suitable meter ranges and never connect an ammeter directly across the supply.
(c) Table (1): Current / A; Potential difference / V; repeat readings in separate columns.

(c) Analysis/conclusion (1): With potential difference vertically against current, the slope is resistance, 12 Ω, at approximately fixed temperature. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

Accept a physically equivalent operational method using suitable named equipment. Do not award a second graph-construction mark in (c). For later calculations, allow error carried forward from a plausible measured gradient when the subsequent relation is correct; do not reward a reversed axis interpretation. items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. What is power?
A. Energy per charge
B. Energy transfer per time
C. Charge per time
D. Total energy regardless of time

2. What does kWh measure?
A. Power per hour
B. Current
C. Resistance
D. Energy

3. Why use parallel lamps for independent lighting?
A. Each must receive half the voltage
B. Current is consumed before the second lamp
C. Each branch can be switched separately
D. One broken branch must stop every other

4. Where is the single-pole switch placed in the model?
A. Neutral conductor only
B. Both ends of a short bypass around the lamp
C. Live conductor
D. Protective earth conductor

5. Which marking commonly identifies double insulation?
A. One square alone
B. Earth terminal symbol
C. Class I earthed-case mark
D. A square within a square

6. In the IEC-colour classroom plug model, which colour identifies protective earth?
A. Brown
B. Green/yellow
C. Blue
D. Black

7. Why can damp conditions worsen shock risk?
A. They can lower path resistance
B. Dampness increases body resistance
C. Dampness makes a fuse trip before a shock
D. Dampness reduces all source voltages to zero

8. What power is 10 V at 0.3 A?
A. 10.3 W
B. 33.3 W
C. 0.03 W
D. 3 W

9. What energy is 0.8 kW for 2 h?
A. 1.6 kWh
B. 0.0008 kWh
C. 0.4 kWh
D. 2.8 kWh

10. At an invented N$3 per kWh, what does 2 kWh cost in energy charges?
A. N$6
B. N$5
C. N$1.50
D. N$2

11. A 6 V, 1 A heater runs for 10 s. What energy is transferred?
A. 0.6 J
B. 600 J
C. 60 J
D. 6 J

12. A 440 W training appliance operates at 220 V. Which fuse is suitable in the simple steady-current exercise: 1 A, 3 A, 10 A or 13 A?
A. 13 A
B. 3 A
C. 1 A
D. 10 A
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key B. A: That is voltage. B: It is measured in watts. C: That is current. D: Duration matters for power.

2. Key D. A: That is not its meaning. B: Current uses amperes. C: Resistance uses ohms. D: It is power multiplied by time.

3. Key C. A: The branches span the same two nodes and therefore have equal voltage. B: Charge is conserved. C: An open branch need not break the others. D: That is a series-path problem.

4. Key C. A: Load may remain connected to live. B: This bypasses the load instead of isolating live. C: It disconnects the load from live. D: Must not interrupt the protective path.

5. Key D. A: The recognised mark uses nested squares. B: Identifies protective earth, not double insulation. C: Double-insulated equipment uses different protection. D: It denotes the protective design.

6. Key B. A: Live in that convention. B: This identifies the protective conductor. C: Neutral in the specified colour convention. D: Not green/yellow protective-earth identification.

7. Key A. A: At the same voltage this can allow more current. B: It can lower path resistance. C: Fuse does not guarantee shock prevention. D: Supply may remain hazardous.

8. Key D. A: This adds unlike quantities. B: This divides V by I. C: This divides I by V. D: Use VI.

9. Key A. A: Multiply power by time. B: This mishandles both the time multiplication and the kW-to-kWh use; 0.8×2 is required. C: This divides by time. D: This adds unlike quantities.

10. Key A. A: Multiply energy by the given tariff. B: This adds values with unlike units. C: This divides tariff by energy. D: This ignores tariff.

11. Key C. A: This divides by duration. B: This adds an extra factor of ten. C: Use VIt. D: This omits duration.

12. Key B. A: It is not the smallest suitable given option. B: This is the stated school selection criterion. C: It is below normal current. D: A smaller suitable option is given.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark for the correct option in each question, for 12 marks total.
Distractor feedback: the canonical answer explains the quantity, mechanism or calculation error behind every wrong option.

items.prompt:
Investigation aim: measure the electrical energy supplied to a low-voltage heater over time. These are invented, idealised practice readings; real readings have scatter.

| Heating time / s | Supplied energy / J |
|---:|---:|
| 0 | 0 |
| 20 | 100 |
| 40 | 200 |
| 60 | 300 |
| 80 | 400 |
| 100 | 500 |

(a) Draw Supplied energy / J vertically against Heating time / s horizontally. Plot the supplied readings and add a separate fitted line. [5]
(b) Show two widely separated points on your fitted line and calculate its gradient. State the gradient unit. [3]
(c) Plan how to measure the electrical energy supplied to a low-voltage heater over time. Name the equipment and arrangement, describe the measurements and repeats, state controls and a relevant precaution, design the results table and explain how the results answer the aim. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Supplied energy / J is vertical and Heating time / s horizontal. Use the six readings, draw a separate best-fit line and show a wide gradient triangle; do not join scattered readings in a zigzag.

Gradient construction: choose the separated fitted-line points (0, 0) and (100, 500). Gradient = (500 − 0) / (100 − 0) = 5 J/s or W. The energy-time slope is electrical input power, 5 W. For comparison, a steady 5 V and 1 A input would give VI = 5 W.

Arrangement: A heater rated for 5 V and 1 A, suitable current-limited supply, voltmeter, ammeter, stopwatch and optional joulemeter

Plan: 1. Place the rated heater in its intended load before connecting the low-voltage circuit. 2. Connect ammeter in series and voltmeter across the heater; verify steady 5 V and 1 A in the example model. 3. Start the stopwatch and record energy using a joulemeter or calculate VIt at each recorded time. 4. Record energy at 20 s intervals over 100 s and monitor V and I for stability. 5. Repeat with the same heater and supply settings, subtracting the initial meter reading if present.
Control and accuracy: Keep supply and heater conditions stable, avoid exposed hot elements, keep electrical connections dry and use no mains construction.
Table: Heating time / s; Supplied energy / J; repeat readings in separate columns. 
Graph and conclusion: The energy-time slope is electrical input power, 5 W. For comparison, a steady 5 V and 1 A input would give VI = 5 W. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

![Original fitted practice graph](assets/practical-6118-24.png)
marking_guidance: (a) Correct quantities and units on both axes (1); regular usable scales (1); points within half a small square, all six (2) or four/five (1); a separate suitable fitted line (1).

(b) A visible wide triangle or two stated separated line coordinates (1); difference in vertical coordinates divided by difference in horizontal coordinates, with correct sign and result (1); unit J/s or W or a stated equivalent derived from vertical unit / horizontal unit (1).
(c) Equipment/arrangement (1): A heater rated for 5 V and 1 A, suitable current-limited supply, voltmeter, ammeter, stopwatch and optional joulemeter

(c) Measurements (3): One mark each for: Connect ammeter in series and voltmeter across the heater; verify steady 5 V and 1 A in the example model.; Record energy at 20 s intervals over 100 s and monitor V and I for stability.; Repeat with the same heater and supply settings, subtracting the initial meter reading if present.

(c) Controls/precaution (2): one mark for a named variable AND how it is kept fixed; one for another specific control or a relevant precaution with its action. Keep supply and heater conditions stable, avoid exposed hot elements, keep electrical connections dry and use no mains construction.
(c) Table (1): Heating time / s; Supplied energy / J; repeat readings in separate columns.

(c) Analysis/conclusion (1): The energy-time slope is electrical input power, 5 W. For comparison, a steady 5 V and 1 A input would give VI = 5 W. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

Accept a physically equivalent operational method using suitable named equipment. Do not award a second graph-construction mark in (c). For later calculations, allow error carried forward from a plausible measured gradient when the subsequent relation is correct; do not reward a reversed axis interpretation. Proposed teaching rubric, not a reconstructed official mark scheme.

items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. What do unlike magnetic poles do?
A. Attract
B. Attract only if one magnet is unmagnetised
C. Repel
D. No interaction at any separation

2. What changes during magnetisation in the dipole model?
A. New magnetic atoms created
B. Alignment decreases
C. Alignment increases
D. All negative charge moves to N pole

3. Which pair is ferromagnetic under ordinary conditions?
A. Nickel and cobalt
B. Copper and aluminium
C. Iron and copper
D. Cobalt and aluminium

4. Why is soft iron useful for a switched electromagnet?
A. It retains strong magnetism after switch-off
B. It magnetises and demagnetises readily
C. It must be mechanically rotated to magnetise
D. It blocks the coil current

5. What shape is the field around a long straight wire?
A. Radial lines from wire
B. Concentric circles
C. Axial lines only inside wire
D. Straight parallel lines normal to wire

6. What does a split-ring commutator do in the simple motor?
A. Reverses coil current each half-turn
B. Maintains unchanging connection of each end
C. Increases field strength each half-turn
D. Reverses supply polarity outside the motor

7. What input does a generator require?
A. Electrical work into the coil as a motor
B. Chemical energy from consuming magnet
C. Mechanical work
D. Thermal input directly without motion

8. An object is attracted to a magnet. What can be concluded?
A. It must be non-ferrous copper
B. It must repel the other pole
C. It may be magnetised or merely magnetisable
D. It must be a permanent magnet

9. Current is out of the page and field rightward. Which way is force?
A. Along the current
B. Downward
C. Along the field
D. Upward

10. Reverse a straight wire’s current. What happens to its magnetic field?
A. It disappears despite current
B. Circles become straight radial lines
C. Circle radius alone reverses while direction stays fixed
D. Circular direction reverses

11. More turns are added but current falls. What is needed for the simple turns comparison?
A. Assume torque must increase by any amount
B. Hold current and other relevant conditions fixed
C. Keep supply voltage fixed and assume current unchanged
D. Ignore winding resistance

12. A short empirical test gives lifting force 0.4 N at 0.2 A and 0.8 N at 0.4 A. What is the secant gradient?
A. 0.5 A/N
B. 0.4 N/A
C. 0.08 N/A
D. 2 N/A
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key A. A: N and S attract. B: Unlike existing poles attract. C: Like poles repel, unlike attract. D: Fields exert force at suitable separation.

2. Key C. A: Existing atomic effects align. B: Magnetisation increases net alignment. C: Net cancellation decreases. D: Magnetic poles are not separated electric charge.

3. Key A. A: These are standard examples. B: Not ferromagnetic in this ordinary comparison. C: Copper is not the required ferromagnetic partner. D: Aluminium is not the required partner.

4. Key B. A: That makes release harder. B: This suits on-off action. C: Coil field magnetises it. D: Core is not selected to block current.

5. Key B. A: Magnetic field circles the current. B: They surround the current axis. C: Field exists outside too. D: Not a long-wire field pattern.

6. Key A. A: This preserves the rotational torque sense. B: That describes slip rings. C: Its main function is current reversal. D: Split ring switches coil connections internally.

7. Key C. A: Generator output comes from mechanical input. B: Magnet is not fuel. C: This supplies its electrical output energy. D: Stated generator needs changing field linkage through motion.

8. Key C. A: That is not supported. B: Unmagnetised iron can be attracted to either. C: Attraction alone cannot distinguish these. D: Induced attraction is an alternative.

9. Key D. A: Force is perpendicular in this setup. B: That reverses one required direction. C: It is perpendicular to the field. D: The left-hand rule gives this direction.

10. Key D. A: A field remains with reversed direction. B: Shape remains circular. C: Reversing current reverses field direction; radius is a location, not a signed direction. D: The right-hand rule changes sense.

11. Key B. A: Current reduction can matter. B: Otherwise two effects change together. C: Extra winding resistance can change current even at fixed voltage. D: It can alter current.

12. Key D. A: This is the reciprocal. B: This omits the current interval. C: This multiplies changes. D: Force change 0.4 N divided by current change 0.2 A.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark for the correct option in each question, for 12 marks total.
Distractor feedback: the canonical answer explains the quantity, mechanism or calculation error behind every wrong option.

items.prompt:
Original structured practice. Answer the parts with working and units where needed.

(a) State the interaction of like poles. [1]

(b) Name a ferromagnetic element other than iron. [1]

(c) Explain magnetisation in the dipole model. [2]

(d) Explain why the coil current reverses each half-turn in a simple DC motor. [2]

(e) Explain the expected effect of increased current at fixed coil geometry and external field. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Repulsion.

(b) Nickel.

(c) More atomic magnetic effects align. Their fields cancel less and give a net magnetic effect.

(d) The coil sides exchange positions. Reversing current keeps the torque in the same rotational sense.

(e) Magnetic side forces increase. Their couple produces a larger turning effect within the operating range.
marking_guidance: (a) One mark for repel.
(b) One mark for nickel or cobalt.
(c) One mark for alignment; one for net effect.
(d) One mark for changed side positions; one for preserved torque sense.
(e) One mark for larger forces; one for larger moment.
Eight marks total; use the definition, reason or working requested by each part.

items.prompt:
Investigation aim: test electromagnet pull as current changes at fixed geometry. These are invented, idealised practice readings; real readings have scatter.

| Current / A | Lifting force / N |
|---:|---:|
| 0.1 | 0.3 |
| 0.2 | 0.5 |
| 0.3 | 0.7 |
| 0.4 | 0.9 |
| 0.5 | 1.1 |
| 0.6 | 1.3 |

(a) Draw Lifting force / N vertically against Current / A horizontally. Plot the supplied readings and add a separate fitted line. [5]
(b) Show two widely separated points on your fitted line and calculate its gradient. State the gradient unit. [3]
(c) Plan how to test electromagnet pull as current changes at fixed geometry. Name the equipment and arrangement, describe the measurements and repeats, state controls and a relevant precaution, design the results table and explain how the results answer the aim. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Lifting force / N is vertical and Current / A horizontal. Use the six readings, draw a separate best-fit line and show a wide gradient triangle; do not join scattered readings in a zigzag.

Gradient construction: choose the separated fitted-line points (0.1, 0.3) and (0.6, 1.3). Gradient = (1.3 − 0.3) / (0.6 − 0.1) = 2 N/A. The slope is the measured change in pull per current over this limited illustrative range, 2 N/A. The 0.1 N intercept can include a force-gauge zero offset; it is not a universal force law.

Arrangement: An insulated coil on a soft-iron core, current-limited low-voltage supply, ammeter, force gauge and the same steel target

Plan: 1. Clamp the insulated coil and soft-iron core and position the same steel target at a marked gap. 2. Check the force gauge zero, record any offset and connect a current-limited supply through the coil and ammeter. 3. Set 0.10 A and pull the target using the gauge in the same direction until it detaches; record the peak force. 4. Repeat at several currents to 0.60 A, switching off between readings to reduce heating. 5. Repeat each pull at the same contact position and retain the raw readings before applying any zero correction.
Control and accuracy: Keep turns, core, gap, target and alignment fixed; limit heating and prevent the target falling onto hands or feet.
Table: Current / A; Lifting force / N; repeat readings in separate columns. 
Graph and conclusion: The slope is the measured change in pull per current over this limited illustrative range, 2 N/A. The 0.1 N intercept can include a force-gauge zero offset; it is not a universal force law. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

![Original fitted practice graph](assets/practical-6118-25.png)
marking_guidance: (a) Correct quantities and units on both axes (1); regular usable scales (1); points within half a small square, all six (2) or four/five (1); a separate suitable fitted line (1).

(b) A visible wide triangle or two stated separated line coordinates (1); difference in vertical coordinates divided by difference in horizontal coordinates, with correct sign and result (1); unit N/A or a stated equivalent derived from vertical unit / horizontal unit (1).
(c) Equipment/arrangement (1): An insulated coil on a soft-iron core, current-limited low-voltage supply, ammeter, force gauge and the same steel target

(c) Measurements (3): One mark each for: Check the force gauge zero, record any offset and connect a current-limited supply through the coil and ammeter.; Repeat at several currents to 0.60 A, switching off between readings to reduce heating.; Repeat each pull at the same contact position and retain the raw readings before applying any zero correction.

(c) Controls/precaution (2): one mark for a named variable AND how it is kept fixed; one for another specific control or a relevant precaution with its action. Keep turns, core, gap, target and alignment fixed; limit heating and prevent the target falling onto hands or feet.
(c) Table (1): Current / A; Lifting force / N; repeat readings in separate columns.

(c) Analysis/conclusion (1): The slope is the measured change in pull per current over this limited illustrative range, 2 N/A. The 0.1 N intercept can include a force-gauge zero offset; it is not a universal force law. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

Accept a physically equivalent operational method using suitable named equipment. Do not award a second graph-construction mark in (c). For later calculations, allow error carried forward from a plausible measured gradient when the subsequent relation is correct; do not reward a reversed axis interpretation. Proposed teaching rubric, not a reconstructed official mark scheme.

items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. A magnet is held stationary inside a stationary coil. What is expected after transients?
A. Alternating output with no motion
B. No sustained induced e.m.f. from the unchanged field
C. Constant induced emf from constant field
D. A pulse every second without a changing field

2. What does Lenz’s law oppose?
A. All movement even when no circuit current flows
B. The change causing induction
C. The direction of the existing current for that interaction
D. The inducing field for that interaction

3. What preserves connection to each rotating AC coil end?
A. Short circuit joining both ends
B. Two brushes on one shared ring
C. Split-ring commutator
D. Separate continuous slip rings

4. What supplies the changing core field in a simple transformer?
A. Alternating primary current
B. Permanent magnet stationary in core
C. Steady primary DC after switch-on
D. Secondary load current alone without input

5. At fixed power, why raise transmission voltage?
A. To lower current and line heating
B. To raise line resistance
C. To increase transmitted power without input
D. To raise line current

6. Which is a common underground-cable advantage?
A. Lower initial installation cost for a typical route
B. Less visual impact
C. Easier visual location of every fault
D. Better heat removal than open air in every soil

7. What energy input drives a generator?
A. Electrical input without motion
B. Energy from slip-ring friction
C. Stored magnet energy consumed as fuel
D. Mechanical input

8. Np = 200, Ns = 100 and Vp = 8 V. What is ideal Vs?
A. 8 V
B. 0.5 V
C. 16 V
D. 4 V

9. An ideal transformer supplies 12 W at 3 V. What output current flows?
A. 12 A
B. 0.25 A
C. 4 A
D. 36 A

10. Rotation rate doubles in the fixed-field two-pole model. What happens to period?
A. It becomes one quarter
B. It doubles
C. It halves
D. It stays fixed

11. The magnet’s motion through a closed coil is reversed. What changes?
A. Induced polarity reverses
B. Current becomes DC in one direction through both strokes
C. Polarity stays fixed
D. Induced emf stays zero despite moving through a changing field

12. At fixed primary conditions, secondary turns double. What is ideal output voltage?
A. Unchanged
B. Half as large
C. Twice as large
D. Four times as large
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key B. A: No periodic change is present. B: Induction requires changing linkage. C: Induction needs changing linkage. D: Unchanged field does not time periodic pulses.

2. Key B. A: Mechanical opposition depends on the induced response. B: This is its directional rule. C: Opposition concerns change, not all current. D: Induced field can reinforce a field that is decreasing.

3. Key D. A: Prevents separate output collection. B: Shorts the two ends rather than keeping separate contacts. C: Swaps connections every half-turn. D: They do not interchange coil ends.

4. Key A. A: It creates changing linkage. B: Unchanging field does not sustain induction. C: Steady field gives no continued secondary emf. D: Does not provide source energy.

5. Key A. A: The reduced current reduces resistive loss. B: That increases losses for a given I. C: Transformers do not create power. D: At fixed P increasing V lowers I.

6. Key B. A: Underground installation commonly costs more. B: Large overhead structures are avoided along the cable route. C: Buried faults are less accessible. D: Thermal conditions depend on burial environment.

7. Key D. A: That is motor operation. B: Friction is a loss, not useful source. C: Magnets are not the ongoing input fuel. D: Rotation requires work.

8. Key D. A: Turns differ. B: That is the turns fraction without applying voltage. C: This reverses the ratio. D: The secondary has half the turns.

9. Key C. A: This ignores voltage. B: This reverses the ratio. C: Use I = P/V. D: This multiplies power and voltage.

10. Key C. A: A factor-two frequency increase gives factor-two, not factor-four, period decrease. B: This reverses the frequency relation. C: Rotation frequency doubles, so period T=1/f halves. D: The repetition rate changed.

11. Key A. A: The linkage change has the opposite sense. B: Reversed magnet motion reverses polarity and current direction in the same closed circuit. C: The direction of field change has reversed. D: The moving magnet can produce a nonzero induced emf.

12. Key C. A: The turns ratio changed. B: That reverses the turns effect. C: Vs scales directly with Ns under the fixed primary conditions. D: The ideal relation is linear.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark for the correct option in each question, for 12 marks total.
Distractor feedback: the canonical answer explains the quantity, mechanism or calculation error behind every wrong option.

Original structured practice. Answer the parts with working and units where needed.

(a) Name the rotating contact arrangement in the simple AC coil generator. [1]

(b) State why steady DC is unsuitable for sustained output from the simple transformer. [1]

(c) Explain the loss advantage of higher transmission voltage at fixed power. [2]

(d) Calculate Vs for Vp = 10 V, Np = 200 and Ns = 80. [2]

items.canonical_answer:

(b) It gives no continuing change of core field after the transient.

(c) Current is lower. Resistive heating in the same line is reduced.

(d) Vs = 10 × 80/200 = 4 V.

(e) Is = P/Vs = 2 A.

(b) One mark for absence of changing linkage.
(c) One mark for lower current; one for lower heating.
(d) One mark for turns ratio; one for 4 V.
(e) One mark for power divided by voltage; one for 2 A.

items.prompt:
Investigation aim: test secondary voltage against turn count with fixed primary conditions. These are invented, idealised practice readings; real readings have scatter.

| Secondary turns | Secondary voltage / V |
|---:|---:|
| 20 | 1 |
| 40 | 2 |
| 60 | 3 |
| 80 | 4 |
| 100 | 5 |
| 120 | 6 |

(a) Draw Secondary voltage / V vertically against Secondary turns horizontally. Plot the supplied readings and add a separate fitted line. [5]
(b) Show two widely separated points on your fitted line and calculate its gradient. State the gradient unit. [3]
(c) Plan how to test secondary voltage against turn count with fixed primary conditions. Name the equipment and arrangement, describe the measurements and repeats, state controls and a relevant precaution, design the results table and explain how the results answer the aim. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
Graph: Secondary voltage / V is vertical and Secondary turns horizontal. Use the six readings, draw a separate best-fit line and show a wide gradient triangle; do not join scattered readings in a zigzag.

Gradient construction: choose the separated fitted-line points (20, 1) and (120, 6). Gradient = (6 − 1) / (120 − 20) = 0.05 V per turn. The slope is secondary voltage per turn, 0.05 V per turn, equal to Vp/Np in the ideal model. These open-circuit readings do not measure efficiency.

Arrangement: A purpose-built low-voltage AC transformer kit, fixed primary winding and core, selectable secondary turns and AC voltmeters

Plan: 1. Set up the fixed primary and iron core of the low-voltage AC transformer kit with the supply off. 2. Select a known secondary turn count and connect an AC voltmeter across that winding. 3. Switch on the rated low AC supply and record both primary and secondary voltages. 4. Switch off, change the secondary turns and repeat with the same core and primary settings. 5. Repeat each setting and check that primary voltage remains constant.
Control and accuracy: Use rated insulated classroom equipment, keep the core assembly consistent, avoid shorted turns and switch off before changing windings.
Table: Secondary turns; Secondary voltage / V; repeat readings in separate columns. 
Graph and conclusion: The slope is secondary voltage per turn, 0.05 V per turn, equal to Vp/Np in the ideal model. These open-circuit readings do not measure efficiency. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

![Original fitted practice graph](assets/practical-6118-26.png)
marking_guidance: (a) Correct quantities and units on both axes (1); regular usable scales (1); points within half a small square, all six (2) or four/five (1); a separate suitable fitted line (1).

(b) A visible wide triangle or two stated separated line coordinates (1); difference in vertical coordinates divided by difference in horizontal coordinates, with correct sign and result (1); unit V per turn or a stated equivalent derived from vertical unit / horizontal unit (1).
(c) Equipment/arrangement (1): A purpose-built low-voltage AC transformer kit, fixed primary winding and core, selectable secondary turns and AC voltmeters

(c) Measurements (3): One mark each for: Select a known secondary turn count and connect an AC voltmeter across that winding.; Switch off, change the secondary turns and repeat with the same core and primary settings.; Repeat each setting and check that primary voltage remains constant.

(c) Controls/precaution (2): one mark for a named variable AND how it is kept fixed; one for another specific control or a relevant precaution with its action. Use rated insulated classroom equipment, keep the core assembly consistent, avoid shorted turns and switch off before changing windings.
(c) Table (1): Secondary turns; Secondary voltage / V; repeat readings in separate columns.

(c) Analysis/conclusion (1): The slope is secondary voltage per turn, 0.05 V per turn, equal to Vp/Np in the ideal model. These open-circuit readings do not measure efficiency. Compare repeated readings and report the tested range rather than claiming an exact law from scattered observations.

Accept a physically equivalent operational method using suitable named equipment. Do not award a second graph-construction mark in (c). For later calculations, allow error carried forward from a plausible measured gradient when the subsequent relation is correct; do not reward a reversed axis interpretation. Proposed teaching rubric, not a reconstructed official mark scheme.

items.prompt:
Choose one correct option for each original practice question.

1. Which particles are nucleons?
A. Protons and neutrons
B. Protons and photons
C. Protons and electrons
D. Neutrons and electrons

2. What fixes an element’s identity?
A. Neutron number
B. Nucleon number alone
C. Proton number
D. Electron number alone

3. Which pair can be isotopes?
A. Same Z, different A
B. Different Z, same A
C. Different electric charge only
D. Same neutrons, different protons

4. What is an alpha particle?
A. Two neutrons without protons
B. Two protons and two neutrons
C. Two protons without neutrons
D. One proton and one neutron

5. What makes a tracer useful for locating a leak?
A. It permanently stops fluid flow
B. It is detected by weighing the pipe
C. It gives no emission outside pipe
D. It follows the fluid and can be detected

6. A sheet becomes thicker under a fixed suitable transmission monitor. What is expected?
A. Unchanged count for every thickness
B. Count equal to source mass
C. Higher transmitted count
D. Lower transmitted count

7. Carbon-14 dating is most directly suited to which model sample?
A. Once-living carbon-containing material
B. Ancient pure metal containing no carbon
C. Fresh volcanic rock with no biological carbon history
D. A modern synthetic sheet with no known carbon source

8. A = 23 and Z = 11. How many neutrons?
A. 23
B. 12
C. 34
D. 11

9. Alpha decay starts with A = 210 and Z = 84. What are daughter numbers?
A. A = 214, Z = 86
B. A = 208, Z = 80
C. A = 210, Z = 85
D. A = 206, Z = 82

10. Beta-minus decay starts with A = 14 and Z = 6. What daughter results?
A. A = 10, Z = 4
B. A = 13, Z = 6
C. A = 14, Z = 7
D. A = 14, Z = 5

11. Atoms have 6 protons each and 6 or 8 neutrons. What follows?
A. Both must be radioactive by definition
B. They are isotopes
C. Their A is equal
D. They are different elements

12. A simple dating model leaves one quarter of initial activity. How many half-lives elapsed?
A. Three
B. Four
C. Two
D. One
items.canonical_answer:
1. Key A. A: They constitute the nucleus. B: Photons are not nucleons. C: Electrons are outside the nucleus. D: Electrons are not nucleons.

2. Key C. A: Isotopes vary N without changing element. B: Different elements can have same A. C: This is atomic number Z. D: Ionisation changes electrons, not element.

3. Key A. A: They share element identity but differ in neutrons. B: They are different elements. C: That can describe ions of the same nuclide. D: Different protons mean different elements.

4. Key B. A: Alpha also has charge +2. B: It is a helium-4 nucleus. C: Alpha contains two neutrons too. D: This is not helium-4 nucleus.

5. Key D. A: Tracer should follow fluid. B: Radiation detection reveals route. C: Escaping signal is the detection clue. D: Its movement and signal reveal location.

6. Key D. A: Suitable radiation is attenuated. B: Counts measure detected radiation, not mass directly. C: More material attenuates more. D: More radiation is attenuated.

7. Key A. A: Its post-exchange decay supplies the clock. B: No relevant C14 reservoir. C: Not the simple C14 organic-sample model. D: The simple calibrated once-living model does not apply directly.

8. Key B. A: This is total nucleons. B: Subtract Z from A. C: This adds instead of subtracting. D: This is proton count.

9. Key D. A: That adds the emitted particle instead of removing it. B: The subtractions are incorrect. C: That is the beta-minus change. D: Subtract four and two.

10. Key C. A: That is the alpha change. B: Nucleon count is unchanged. C: A neutron becomes a proton. D: That is the wrong beta-minus charge direction.

11. Key B. A: Isotope does not imply radioactivity. B: They have common Z and different A. C: Their neutron numbers differ. D: Their Z is equal.

12. Key C. A: Three half-lives leave one eighth, not one quarter. B: That leaves one sixteenth. C: One half then one quarter. D: That leaves one half.
marking_guidance: Key: one mark for the correct option in each question, for 12 marks total.
Distractor feedback: the canonical answer explains the quantity, mechanism or calculation error behind every wrong option.

items.prompt:
Original structured practice. Answer the parts with working and units where needed.

(a) State what Z counts. [1]

(b) State what A counts. [1]

(c) Explain why carbon-12 and carbon-14 are isotopes. [2]

(d) Calculate daughter A and Z for alpha decay from A = 218, Z = 84. [2]

(e) Calculate daughter A and Z for beta-minus decay from A = 24, Z = 11. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) Protons in the nucleus.

(b) Protons plus neutrons.

(c) They share six protons and therefore element identity. Their nucleon and neutron numbers differ.

(d) A = 214 and Z = 82.

(e) A = 24 and Z = 12.
marking_guidance: (a) One mark for protons.
(b) One mark for total nucleons.
(c) One mark for equal proton number; one for different neutron/nucleon number.
(d) One mark for each correctly reduced number.
(e) One mark for unchanged A; one for Z increased by one.
Eight marks total; use the definition, reason or working requested by each part.

items.prompt: Plan a safe coin investigation modelling radioactive half-life. Include equipment, survivor-count measurements, repeats, fixed rules, a results table and the expected graph.
items.canonical_answer: A tray and at least 100 identical coins form the model. The initial count is recorded. The remaining coins are shaken and tossed each round; heads are removed and tails counted. Repeating with the survivors gives a decreasing count. The whole experiment is repeated with the full initial set using the same head-removal rule and tossing method. A table records round number and survivors for each run. Mean survivors plotted against round number should fall by about one half per round, with random variation; one round models the half-life, not a measured time in seconds.
marking_guidance: Equipment/arrangement (1): many identical coins and a tray or contained tossing area.
Measurement (1): initial count recorded.
Procedure (1): toss all remaining coins, remove one specified face and count survivors.
Repetition (1): continue with survivors, then repeat the whole run from the full set.
Controls (1): same removal rule and comparable tossing method.
Safety (1): contain loose coins; keep them away from small children and do not use radioactive material.
Table (1): round number and survivor counts for each run.

Graph/conclusion (1): approximately half survive each round with random fluctuations; the graph gives a model half-life of about one round. Accept dice with the correct survival fraction and a fitted model half-life.

(a) State the charge sign of beta-minus radiation. [1]

(b) State whether gamma is deflected by the simple electric-field arrangement. [1]

items.canonical_answer:
(a) Negative.

(b) It is undeflected.

(c) Individual decays occur randomly. The observed count therefore fluctuates about its expected rate.

(d) Two halvings occur, so half-life = 10/2 = 5 min.

(e) Source rate = 42 − 6 = 36 counts/s.
